Title: Transport and spatial organization of cities: synthesis of theories and models
Author: Michael Wegener
Abstract: The spatial organization of contemporary cities is of bewildering complexity. Urban growth and decline, concentration and dispersal, polarization and equalization, prosperity and deprivation coexist in an intricate spatio-temporal web of partly interdependent and partly autonomous processes. In this paper an overview of classical and contemporary approaches to modeling the interface between spatial interaction and location in urban regions is given. Four paradigms are distinguished: technological, economic, social and political. In a second part of the paper an attempt to integrate components of the four paradigms in an unified theoretical framework and quantitative mode! of the transport and spatial organization in urban regions is presented.

Title: The use of satellite imagery in geography: contributions and limitations
Author: Hassan Ouerdani
Abstract: Remote sensing represents an evolution in methods of spatial analysis, planning, and management. The digital nature of its data, its extensive spatial coverage, and its ease of acquisition are advantages that attract the attention of various users seeking spatial information and integrating it into their work methods. However, its use in geography, in its current state, remains very limited due to a lack of the necessary material and technical resources for its development.

Title: Remote sensing as an aid to landscape diagnosis in West Africa
Author: Magatte Ba
Abstract: In Western Senegal, where rural populations are densely populated, numerous studies highlight the degradation of the biophysical environment. The need for an "integrated" or "comprehensive" approach makes landscape the primary focus of study. Remote sensing offers geographers new resources: with its high spatial resolution (30m x 30m) and spectral characteristics (particularly in the near-infrared), the Thematic Mapper image provided by the Landsat-5 satellite allows for a suitable assessment of landscapes. The homogeneous colors resulting from multiband analyses carried out in two test areas (color composites and supervised classifications), which can be identified on the ground, provide information on rural areas that are more or less vulnerable and give an idea of the available land and vegetation resources.

Title: Mapping invisibility: the development of a RIA site
Author: Laurence Ledu
Abstract: Landscape laws, landscape charters, landscape plans... the landscape has long since transcended the realm of the painting to become a consumer good, a heritage to be managed, a legislative theme, a planning criterion, and an advertising image. The demands placed upon landscape call for specific reflection and methodologies. Before any potential assessment, it is essential to describe, understand, and comprehend these landscapes: the use of remote sensing provides a synthetic view, while the overlaying of satellite images onto Digital Terrain Models reintroduces the effect of relief. On this topic, the analysis and mapping of intervisibility is crucial: which spaces are visible and which are hidden, and in what proportions? How do they evolve in response to development projects and the observer's movements? The project developed from the landscaping of the Château de la Roche Jagu Park (Côtes d'Armor) illustrates the possibilities offered by these techniques and the complexity of such a system.

Title: The IRISOS process
Author: Charles Schneider
Abstract: Introducing a new graphic method for spatial description. The IRISOS process results in the graphic reconstruction of the spectral components of a surface. It can be considered as a correspondence between two interference systems: color, which is equivalent to light interference, and the surface, considered as a result of the interference of spatial waves. The spectral redefinition of color leads to a change in the way the surface is perceived.

Title: SADIC: Decision Support System in Cartographic Computing
Author: Dominique Laffly, Pascal Gillon
Abstract: SADIC is software that manages and filters information on large thematic databases. It intervenes upstream in the information processing, thus enabling the rapid validation or refutation of working hypotheses. Its principle is based on ease of use in terms of choosing units and levels of spatial aggregation, the data to be represented, and the methods of statistical analysis, thanks to a user-friendly graphical interface and the rapid formatting of cartographic results. SADIC is developed to be easily adaptable and scalable, particularly to integrate the temporal dimension and to be portable to other information sources.

Title: For a model of spatial differentiation
Author: Jean-Pierre Chéry
Abstract: The concept of differentiated space is one of the cornerstones of geographical discourse. Spatial differentiation appears as a complex process whose formalization is not yet satisfactory. A systemic approach seems to be a relevant framework for modeling this process. A model simulating this process is discussed within the context of the territorial functioning of a differentiated space. The modeling approach, starting from concepts describing the object to be modeled—here, a cross-border space—encounters difficulties in formalization. Forresterian modeling, through systems dynamics, is an approach that has made it possible to develop models of homogeneous spaces. The possibilities of using this method for spatial differentiation are presented.

Title: Models for decision support: the case of the housing market in a border region (Morteau, Doubs)
Author: Alexandre Moine
Abstract: This article serves as a preamble to the development of a model for the functioning of a housing market considered within a local context and subject to the specific influence of a border. The housing market is known to be particularly complex. It can be considered a system composed of interacting heterogeneous elements. The proposed approach, based on systems dynamics, allows us to take into account both the temporal and spatial dimensions of the phenomenon. However, we observe that using the simulation results provided by the model is difficult. To become a decision-support tool, the model must be complemented by a knowledge-based system, used as an interactive decision support system.

Title: Local development, employment and planning impacts: elements for an interactive decision support system
Author: Jean-Marie Chekhab
Abstract: Local development is undeniably part of the current conceptual framework, with its emphasis on prioritizing employment. However, faced with the need to manage the main economic developments within their territories, decision-makers increasingly feel the need to rationalize their decision-making. This necessitates the creation of a tool to inform and assist them in their endeavors. We propose to present the elements necessary for creating an interactive decision-support system for localized employment management and the impacts of development projects. This system will be developed using systems dynamics and interfaced with a knowledge-based system to explain the model's results.

Title: Modeling dynamic traffic flow in networks
Author: Martin Hilliges
Abstract: In this paper a simulation model for time dependent traffic flow in networks with multiple sources and sinks is presented. The main goals are the real-time simulation of large highway networks and the development of a planning tool for traffic networks. First, the assumptions beyond the model are presented. Second, I describe the adaptation of the mode! to numerical simulations and the constructions of networks. The next sections contain a short note on decision processes and our approach to this field. Then an extension of the model to a larger framework, and possible fields of application are proposed. In the Iast section a simulation of the traffic flow in a network is shown.

Title: Simulation of regional dynamic processes in the economy
Author: Kai Brandt
Abstract: Economical interactions between countries or regions of countries become more and more important for the economy of nations, the EC and the whole world. Nevertheless, there are only few attempts to model these processes, because most of the classical economic models are too unhandy or too stiff to be extended on regional effects. My approach to this problem is bases upon the dynamic choice theories developed by G. Haag and W. Weidlich from the University of Stuttgart. It describes the behavior of demand, supply and prices due to the choice behavior of consumers and producers. It is built up modular, so that it can easily be fit to the requirements of single branches or products. Thus it cannot be applied to political economics as a whole but it can teach us some astonishing effects in parts of them.

Title: Analytical method for modeling slope deposits in high mountain areas
Author: Pierre Pech
Abstract: Slope deposits (scree and other boulders) cover significant areas in high mountain regions, particularly in the Dévoluy massif. Analysis of morphometric, sedimentological, biogeographic, and spatial parameters allows us to propose quantified models for defining slope deposits. These models are compared to the morphodynamic processes observed in the slope deposits. Fluctuations in the values of the slope deposit models correspond to variations in morphogenic dynamics.

Title: The use of the analysis of variance model in geographical research
Author: Cécile Helle
Abstract: Within the framework of the analysis of the building plot market in the Vaucluse region, we propose to test the potential contributions (particularly compared to the methods classically used in this type of study: multivariate linear regression model, etc.) of analysis of variance. Two research areas are prioritized: - the variance model as an explanatory tool for the spatial differentiation of building plot prices (thanks, among other things, to a better consideration of spatial discontinuities), - the variance model as a verification tool, following an inductive approach to data processing that led to the projection of a spatial organization model onto a structure observed in reality.

Title: New time-space maps of Europe
Author: Klaus Speikermann
Abstract: Increasing mobility is one of the constituting characteristics of modemity. Toda y, Europe is facing a new thrust of acceleration: the planned European high-speed rail network will open up new dimensions on travel speed and so of the relation of space and time. The topic of the paper is the visualization of the new relationship of space and time by a new type of maps. These time-space maps do not display distances but time distances between cities and countries. For this purpose a method for creating time-space maps has been developed, which improves current methods and avoids their pitfalls. To demonstrate the developed method, time-space maps for Europe, France and German are presented there.

Title: Image analysis and boundary effect: spatio-temporal analysis of settlement patterns in the Pyrenean regions
Author: Sandra Perez
Abstract: This contribution presents the approach used to detect the impact of the Pyrenean border on recent population trends in the municipalities of Pyrénées-Orientales and Girona. Statistical analyses are performed using measurements obtained through image analysis, resulting in spatial modeling.

Title: Characterizing the evolution of a network of facility usage through fractal analysis
Author: Jean-Luc Bonnefoy
Abstract: Municipal inventories (1979 and 1988) allow for the construction of graphs showing the frequency of visits to shops and services. These graphs, created within a geographic information system, overlay two types of inter-municipal relationships: nested hierarchies with increasingly populated municipalities and increasingly scarce shops and services, and a network of cooperation or complementarity between smaller municipalities. The fractal dimension quantifies the internal hierarchical structures and, in this case, allows for the quantification of trends in the network of facility visits.

Title: Methodological problems posed by an expert-system approach in geography
Author: Nathalie Dubus
Abstract: Expert systems are designed to replicate the reasoning of an expert in a particular field. Their use as a decision-support tool can be considered in geography. The process for developing an expert system consists of several stages: identification, learning, modeling, knowledge formalization and computerization, followed by validation and enrichment of the model. Strong interactions exist between knowledge modeling and the tool used. While this tool offers certain advantages, it also raises fundamental and formal problems in the representation and processing of knowledge. This is highlighted by the development of an expert system for decision support in water planning in the Sahel region.

Title: Knowledge bases and methods: coupled systems
Author: Franck Guarniéry, Jean-Luc Wybo
Abstract: Regardless of the application domain, many problems require technical solutions that combine methods from artificial intelligence and traditional computer science. This contribution aims to present the concept of a Problem-Solving Environment. This concept is closely linked to that of numerical-symbol coupling in modeling, as well as to the integration of knowledge from experts in a particular domain and/or from experts in different domains.

Title: SIMPOP, a multi-agent model for the evolution of population systems
Author: France Guérin-Pace, Hélène Mathian, Denise Pumain, Lena Sanders, Stéphane Bura
Abstract: Multi-agent systems, a branch of distributed artificial intelligence, offer great flexibility for modeling the dynamics of complex systems. Traditional methods used to reproduce dynamics employ formalization through a system of differential equations. Modeling by multi-agent systems relies on a set of rules, combining qualitative knowledge and quantitative information, which allows for the simultaneous manipulation of different and nested geographical scales: the level of individuals (microscopic level), cities (meso), and the macroscopic level of a territory. Mechanisms already known to govern growth processes and spatial interactions, such as the effects of competition, the deterrent effect of distance, or the contraction of space-time, are incorporated into the system's operating rules. The objective of the model presented here is to reproduce, over a very long period (approximately two thousand years), the transition from a relatively homogeneous settlement system with an agricultural economy to a hierarchical urban organization. Different hypotheses are tested using simulations and this tool thus makes it possible to evaluate the respective roles of the parameters that characterize the "components" of cities as well as the effect of the different rules that govern the evolution of the whole system.

Title: The issue of evolving agricultural land use: towards a hybrid system coupled with an object information system
Author: Didier Josselin, Bruno Orsier
Abstract: Hybrid systems that leverage the strengths of neural networks and classical artificial intelligence are currently enjoying great success in computer science. Our research, the result of a multidisciplinary collaboration, aims to combine a GIS with such a hybrid system to address the following problem: modeling the phenomenon of agricultural land abandonment. Our presentation will include: - the critical results of preliminary studies conducted using more traditional techniques (data analysis, symbolic learning, machine learning, etc.), - our motivations and hopes regarding the use of neural networks as an intermediary between Geographic Information Systems, statistical tools, and classical artificial intelligence (current limitations of these tools).

Title: Accessibility network: computer modeling and decision support in planning
Author: Alain Touret, Pierre Dumolard
Abstract: Raster GIS is particularly well-suited to spatial analysis, modeling, and simulation. Therefore, it is beneficial to integrate functions useful for this purpose. Among those that are possible, measuring accessibility within a given space seems fundamental. To build the corresponding module, we used a multi-agent (connectionist) approach and programmed in the object-oriented language C++, which allows for integration with the GRASS GIS, itself written in C.

Title: French employment zones differentiated by employment, training and qualifications
Author: Patrice Card, Dominique Laffly
Abstract: Since the decentralization of state responsibilities for training policies to regional councils, an increasing number of studies have been conducted at the employment zone level. These zones were defined based on studies of commuting patterns and correspond fairly well to the employment catchment areas of French cities. The statistical analysis of various static and dynamic indicators, developed in 1990 by INSEE (the French National Institute of Statistics and Economic Studies) for the 348 defined employment zones, allows for the creation of a typology of these catchment areas, and therefore of French cities. Factor analyses and hierarchical clustering of 18 variables related to employment, education level, training system, and qualifications identified within the zones reveal significant differences between French employment zones. Three distinct Frances emerge, characterized by a dual tension: - industrial France in the East and North contrasts with the high-sector France of major cities, - rural France contrasts with urban France. This quantitative approach to the phenomenon of territorial differentiation through employment and training attempts to shed new light on the role of these factors in the organization of French space.

Title: Motorway observatories: methodology, indicators. Example of the Observatory of the economic effects of the A39 (Dole-Bourg-en-Bresse)
Author: Marie-Agnès Lanneaux
Abstract: Due to the scale of the work required for their construction and, above all, the sums of money involved, highways have always raised questions among decision-makers. In the 1960s in the United States and from the 1970s onward in France, numerous studies sought to measure the effects of a highway on the territory it crosses. The establishment of observatories arose from these questions. This article aims to present the methodological elements developed by the Observatory to measure the economic effects of the A39 motorway on the organization and management of space between Dole and Bourg-en-Bresse.

Title: Diversity in farm operations and spatial organization: towards diagnostic methods using spatial indicators
Author: Isabelle Duvernoy, Françoise Axes
Abstract: The evolution of agriculture is accompanied by transformations of the space under its influence. Using two examples—one on the dynamics of agricultural colonization in an Argentinian province, the other on vineyards in the Béziers region of France—the spatial organization of farms was considered an indicator of their functioning. By employing new tools for obtaining and interpreting geographic information (remote sensing, GIS), methods are proposed to generalize diagnoses and obtain a representation of the local diversity of agricultural activity at a regional scale. This "spatial generalization" requires spatial modeling of the types of agriculture to be differentiated and reflection on the link between levels of agricultural activity organization and their corresponding spatial units. It presents varying degrees of complexity depending on whether the key organizational level, that of the farm, corresponds to a continuous, easily delimited space or to a discontinuous spatial unit.

Title: Spatial approach to the risk of diffuse pollution in intensive agricultural areas: Application to a tributary of the Elorn (Western Brittany)
Author: Monique Launay, Laurence Hubert-moy
Abstract: The study begins with the observation of the degradation of the marine ecosystem in the Brest harbor: the diffuse pollution of agricultural origin in the Elorn River and its tributaries is the focus of the analysis. Nitrate pollution involves factors related to both the environment and agricultural practices. These factors must therefore be considered together to understand their spatial and temporal interactions. The use of a GIS (Arclnfo) enabled the zoning of the watershed based on environmental factors (soils, slopes, etc.) and the definition of risk zones according to agricultural practices. The results obtained allow for the determination of a risk index at the plot level, which is then compared to the risk index obtained using a nitrate leaching model. The problem of extrapolating the method to a larger geographical area is considered, in particular using satellite data: the evaluation of the loss of precision linked to the input parameters available at this new scale is analyzed.

Title: Telematics in the service of geographic information
Author: Serge Leverbe
Abstract: The "Atlas of French Cities" online service provides information on the 231 urban areas (agglomerations) in metropolitan France with a population exceeding 20,000 inhabitants according to the 1990 General Population Census. This project responds to an analysis of the demand for localized geographic information, often expressed in terms of complementarity and comparability. To meet the first requirement, we present the information in the form of maps, data tables, and written commentary. The approach adopted for the second is oriented along two axes: an analysis of similar cities (those in France that exhibit the same characteristics for a given variable) and an analysis of neighboring cities (all the agglomerations in the same region, regardless of their values for the chosen variable).

Title: Analyzing distance in the spatial differentiation of land values: introducing the concepts of spatial covariation and regression
Author: Cécile Helle
Abstract: The fundamental hypothesis of all research on land value formation in urban areas posits that land prices are dependent on distance from the city center. The existence of such a relationship is confirmed in the peri-urban area of Avignon, but the search for secondary explanatory variables raises a number of problems. The set of regressors for the price per square meter (average transaction size, role of real estate professionals in the market, territorial congestion index, etc.) is, in fact, linked to varying degrees of intensity to distance. This identical spatial structure (area gradient) between the dependent variable and the explanatory variables complicates interpretation: the nature of the various covariations is not explicit, and the correlations between the regressors are numerous.

Title: Variographic analysis of satellite data to determine the size of sampling units. Example of a land cover inventory in agricultural and forestry areas
Author: P. Fournier, H. Geroyannis, V. Godard
Abstract: When conducting a land-use inventory and combining the contributions of remote sensing and spatial sampling, the issue of sampling unit size must be addressed. In agricultural areas, this sampling unit is usually based on the average farm size. However, in forested or sparsely populated areas, no similar information exists to calibrate the sampling unit to any particular landscape structure. Variographic analysis of digital satellite data provides a solution to this problem. Because this data is spatially autocorrelated, it is possible to determine the size of landscape features and, therefore, the minimum distance a sampling unit must have to encompass a large number of landscapes. The study focused on two agricultural and two forested areas in the southern Paris Basin. The results indicate that the distances, read from the variograms, suitable for calibrating the sampling units range from 140 to 260 m for forest areas and from 400 to 450 m for agricultural areas. These distances logically differ from one landscape to another and, for comparison, they indicate that the size of the sampling units (720 m), used in 1986 by the Central Service for Surveys and Statistical Studies of the Ministry of Agriculture during an agricultural inventory, is, in this region, oversized relative to the diversity of the landscapes.

Title: Highlighting local discontinuities through principal component analysis of oriented dissimilarities: application to the space of secondary schools in the Paris metropolitan area
Author: Jean-Christophe François
Abstract: This work focuses on analyzing the geographical distribution of local discontinuities within the socio-educational space of the Paris metropolitan area. It examines discontinuities attributable to students' national origins and differences in academic underachievement. Naturally, it seeks to determine whether a certain logic governs the structuring of these geographical discontinuities. The aim is to highlight discontinuities combining several convergent elements. These discontinuities, which are termed structural, are generally more stable, more readily apparent to residents, and less sensitive to individual behavior than other types of discontinuities. The tool proposed for measuring them is a principal component analysis performed not on the attributes of places, but on a series of "oriented dissimilarity" indices describing each of the contact segments between two contiguous spatial units. The objective of the analysis is twofold. The aim is twofold: firstly, to identify, among all the boundaries between contiguous recruitment areas, those that can be classified as structural discontinuities, and secondly, to assess the contribution of different indicators to the formation of these structural discontinuities. The use of this tool required the development of a suitable cartographic representation.

Title: GIS and exploratory analysis: towards new practices in geography
Author: Jean-Marc Orhan
Abstract: The current market for Geographic Information System (GIS) software is vast: over a hundred programs exist, and users routinely work with databases of 300,000 objects. Future needs will lie in the area of data visualization and analysis. The integration of a statistical analysis module into the MacMap GIS, and in particular the creation of a user interface, necessitates the development of new analytical approaches that leverage the capabilities of GIS. The goal is to use cartographic methods to represent results and facilitate their interpretation. The hope is to encourage users to employ statistical tools, but above all, to utilize the spatial management capabilities of GIS to create new spaces based on the analysis results. The objective, therefore, is to develop tools that generate new coordinate systems. From a frequency histogram to a factorial plane or a scatter plot, we are always dealing with one of these recreated spaces. Their cartographic visualization and interaction should offer geographers powerful analytical tools.

Title: Tourism stakeholders and decision-making spaces in Auxois
Author: Valérie Delignières
Abstract: Understanding, evaluating, and analyzing the actions undertaken or proposed by tourism stakeholders in a given rural area: this could summarize the main objectives of this presentation. Based on analyses derived from theoretical foundations and their application to a specific area, the aim is to highlight the strengths and weaknesses of the system, with particular emphasis on the phenomena of nested scales. Indeed, when these phenomena are considered within the overall framework, they allow for an immediate understanding of both the complexity and the major dysfunctions of tourism development processes specific to rural areas.

Title: Modeling housing demand in border areas: an analysis applied to the local market of Morteau (Doubs)
Author: Alexandre Moine
Abstract: It is now widely accepted that local housing markets are complex systems, the analysis of which requires the development of specific methods. The system dynamics method appears particularly well-suited. Here, it is applied to the overall functioning of a local market located in France, in the Franco-Swiss border region. The approach is based on an analysis of the segmentation of the housing stock according to its characteristics and those of its occupants, and on household mobility between these dwellings. Mobility is considered to be influenced by the local employment situation and the specific socio-economic context linked to the border, by household life cycles, their residential strategies, and housing availability. The use of system dynamics allows for the creation of a model representing the evolution of housing demand in relation to household mobility between the different segments. As a decision-making tool, the flexibility of the constructed model allows for the obtaining of very interesting results.

Title: Structuring of regular container ship shipping lines
Author: Olivier Joly
Abstract: Current work focuses on structuring regular shipping line (container) networks to describe container flows and their continuity over time and maritime space. "Establishing a coherent set of measurements for shipping (container) networks," which can be linked to existing measurements for land transport networks (rail, road), was one of the goals set to begin my work on the location of logistics platforms in Northwest Europe. The methodology proposes the construction of measurement indicators specific to container shipping line networks.

Title: A geographical model for analyzing the problems of implementing a large transport infrastructure
Author: Jean Ollivro
Abstract: Increasingly, conflicts arise during infrastructure development projects, pitting decision-makers and operators against local residents. Resolving these conflicts is an extremely daunting task. This paper aims to contribute to resolving these clashes using a thesis on the Mediterranean TGV project and observations made on the Brittany-Pays de la Loire TGV project. Various solutions are discussed, ranging from moderate to radical, depending on whether or not one accepts the current decision-making process in its entirety. These solutions lead to the presentation of a simple geographical model that facilitates a better understanding of the development process.

Title: Knowledge transfer for the implementation of an expert system
Author: Nathalie Dubus
Abstract: Developing an expert system means transferring knowledge from humans to machines. Transcribing particularly complex expert reasoning requires phases of knowledge extraction, modeling, and formalization. Each of these steps will require specific working methods. The knowledge acquisition task is certainly the most complex, the least formal, but also the most interesting in the development of an expert system. Its importance is growing because it determines the quality and relevance of the tool developed and its effectiveness in supporting decision-making in the fields of environment and land-use planning.

Title: AGRIPA: Calculation of access cost by constrained diffusion on a differentiated space using a multi-agent system
Author: Alain Touret
Abstract: This article presents a raster spatial operator for calculating the cost of access to a road network, which we developed at the Alpine Mountain Laboratory (LAMA) in Grenoble. We use a multi-agent system to realistically simulate individual traffic patterns. Several diffusion sources can be considered in competition.

Title: Presentation of a "fuzzy" expert system for the implementation of a local development policy
Author: Sophie de Ruffray
Abstract: The objective is to present the implementation of an expert system as a decision-support tool, emphasizing the spatial and temporal foundations of local development upon which the expert system is based, the advantages and limitations of an expert system approach for decision support in spatial management, and the dual specificity of such a tool, which takes into account both the constraints related to space in general and the problems generated at the micro-scale. To address all these constraints, it is necessary to define and clarify the concept of geographic space, to rigorously formalize the qualitative and quantitative knowledge related to this micro-space using fuzzy logic, and to present evaluation models to aid in the diagnosis of a local development action.

Title: Proposal for a decision support system in an ambiguous environment
Author: Philippe Quarrey, Caroline Berry, Nand Aggarwal
Abstract: In the social sector, and more specifically in career guidance, decision-making often occurs in contexts where information is imprecise and uncertain. Under such conditions, methods for representing and manipulating imperfectly described knowledge must be employed to reflect the flexibility of human reasoning. Decision support techniques are thus adapted for application in uncertain and ambiguous environments. This study was conducted for the Association for Adult Vocational Training (AFPA).

Title: The making of the landscape: from quantitative to qualitative
Author: Jacques Monnier-Raball
Abstract: The concept of landscape is both a representational image and the result of the behavior of social actors within a territory. Landscape is perceived, paradoxically, as both a natural given and a site for development—that is, as a portion of territory to be preserved and as a portion of territory to be transformed. Computer-generated imagery allows for the production of landscape models, the qualitative visualization of which depends on a purely quantitative approach based on digital data. IDERALPE is developing an interactive computer-based decision-support tool, emphasizing the realism of the representation, particularly textures. While the use of such a tool has not yet become widespread, there is every reason to believe that it will soon constitute the essential interface between the various stakeholders—local authorities, developers, decision-makers—and the users of the space.

Title: The geography of writing on screen: new media, new approaches
Author: Madeleine Griselin, Serge Ormaux
Abstract: New information technologies (NICs) are permeating society and thus impacting geography, a social science. Furthermore, the emergence of geography on the internet and CD-ROMs is changing how everyone accesses this field of knowledge. For researchers, this undoubtedly encourages them to conduct their work and disseminate their findings differently. For the general public, specialists in other disciplines, and policymakers, it is certainly an opportunity to change their perspective on geography. We sought to gain a clearer understanding, to characterize (and quantify) the offerings available on online and offline services. What content and image of geography are being conveyed? Is geographical research present? How could it be more so? This presentation aims to frame the immense opportunities offered to our discipline by new media. We will draw on investigations we have conducted using these various media, which represent only the beginning of a more in-depth research project.

Title: Identification of relevant spatial entities for measuring the impact of agricultural activity on the territory
Author: Didier Josselin, Catherine Laurent
Abstract: The idea stemmed from the significant bias affecting the data from the General Agricultural Census. Indeed, the utilized agricultural area of farms is recorded by farm headquarters, and not according to the actual location of the plots. However, it is common knowledge that farmers often use plots outside their municipality. The aim of this work is to provide a new territorial division by aggregating municipalities. The new spatial entities defined must minimize the effects of inter-municipal control.

Title: A corpus of georeferenced data for the management of the physical component of river hydrosystems: the example of the Drôme
Author: Norbert Landon, Hervé Piegay
Abstract: Environmental geographers today provide answers to managers, particularly in the context of river systems. Our team has thus carried out the geomorphological and biogeographical study for the Water Management and Development Plan (SAGE), a pilot project in the Rhône basin, and the Drôme basin. The entire approach is based on the creation of a georeferenced database, the basic unit being a 500-meter section. The variables collected on more than 200 sections come from multiple sources (vertical or oblique aerial photographs, longitudinal profiles). This system has made it possible to: - construct analytical and synthetic maps, that is to say, maps combining several variables (channel incision and potential recharge, diversity of the vegetation mosaic and areas to be conserved or restored as a priority, etc.); - to solve basic research problems by establishing statistical links between variables (abundance of wood jams and bed geometry; importance of bed depth and local recharge; fish and habitat potential).

Title: Towards a quantitative analysis of riparian microlandscapes: presentation of initial results
Author: Mélanie Cossin, Hervé Piegay
Abstract: For about ten years, river managers have been moving towards a so-called holistic management approach, which involves a multidisciplinary perspective. Landscape is considered an important element to manage. However, these managers are not very receptive to the subjective approaches proposed by many consulting firms. A methodological reflection based on a quantitative approach to landscape analysis was therefore initiated to provide managers with an initial framework. Two points will be presented: - the main areas to explore within the framework of an eco-landscape analysis, - the approach implemented at the scale of riparian micro-landscapes. The analysis of the areas occupied by the units of a photographed landscape, carried out using principal component analysis (PCA), makes it possible to identify the micro-landscapes characterizing the river studied (the Rhins in the Beaujolais region).

Title: Nested scales and remote sensing: the ambiguity of the pixel
Author: Christine Allain, Marie Clairay
Abstract: Landscape analysis cannot currently be conducted without clearly mentioning scales, which deserve to be the subject of dedicated research. In the literature, when a particular scale is referred to, it implicitly refers to the area being studied. Geographers readily manipulate scales and increasingly incorporate the transition from one to another, which many authors describe as nested scales. In remote sensing, landscape studies utilize various Earth observation satellites. Each satellite has specific characteristics that determine its spatial and spectral resolution. The resulting images consist of a mosaic of pixels whose content is closely linked to the EIFOV (Effective Instantaneous Field of View). These inter-sensor differences raise questions for geographers regarding the validity of successive nested spaces, as well as the validity of the boundaries of the identified landscape units.

Title: Spatial externalities and location models: simulation on a theoretical network
Author: Marie-Alexandre Laurent
Abstract: This research concerns the introduction of negative spatial externalities into location-allocation models. The location model chosen and extended to incorporate the notion of spatial externality is the p-median model. Different sets of theoretical simulations are performed to test the sensitivity of the solutions proposed by the models to the introduction of spatial externalities. Two point clouds were chosen (rectangular and hexagonal), the network is regular, the demand is homogeneous, and various simple dispersion functions of the externalities are considered. The costs due to negative externalities decrease with distance from the source and are added to the transportation cost.

Title: Space management by logistics organizations in the mass retail sector
Author: Estelle Morcello
Abstract: For the past fifteen years or so, major food retailers have been implementing sophisticated logistics organizations aimed at optimizing the supply of their stores. The central components of these systems are warehouses or distribution centers. The location of these hubs is therefore crucial for understanding the structure of agri-food supply chains (volume, frequency, routes, etc.) across France. The goal of this research is to identify the criteria, both spatial and non-spatial, that determine the form and operation of a logistics organization; this involves finding common rules for applying these criteria and determining the importance of each rule for each of the ten or so retail groups studied.

Title: Maps to reveal mobility on both sides of the middle Rhône since 1975
Author: Stéphane Leroy
Abstract: Even today, the myth of the Rhône as a "border river" continues to haunt the minds of those living along its banks and to influence the decisions of economic and political actors. Based on an analysis of the evolution of trans-Rhône mobility for employment between Valence and Avignon since 1975, this contribution seeks to demonstrate that this idea has run its course and that, while the historical asymmetry between its two banks persists, the Rhône is becoming increasingly permeable and therefore less and less of a structuring force. It is the simplest yet most fundamental tool of geography that allows us to highlight the inevitable "disappearance" of the Rhône: the map (which can be complemented by a graphic model).

Title: Frequency-domain images for urban density analysis
Author: Charles Schneider
Abstract: The proposed contribution is an application of the IRISOS geographic image processing method that I presented at the first Théo Quant Meetings. Starting with a surface of known urban densities, we reconstruct, using a wave-like reference frame, the structure of densification movements, their nesting, and their superposition. We move from the form itself to an image of the processes that account for that form.

Title: Image analysis applied to the study of the spatial diffusion of an innovation: the case of the Itinéris network
Author: Céline Tritz
Abstract: France Télécom, until then the leader in the French telecommunications market, has developed its own mobile telecommunications network, ltinéris, over the past three years. This network is the result of a recent innovation, based on a new digital transmission standard, GSM (Global System for Mobile Telecommunications). The French operator is deploying its network in two ways: technically, by equipping the country, and commercially, with attractive advertising campaigns. Most studies examining network diffusion focus on potential adopters, their distribution, and the spread of the phenomenon. In our study, we use the coverage maps regularly published in the ltinéris booklets to analyze the network's expansion processes. The detection of diffusion patterns and the rules governing equipment deployment was carried out using image analysis and mathematical morphology. The method presented allows for the coupling of different layers of information, but above all, for measurements to be performed using image transformations. Although still in its early stages, it can be applied to all types of spatial data and can be used to describe shapes qualitatively and quantitatively, to determine diffusion rules and, in the context of a prospective study, to quantify the parameters of a probabilistic diffusion model.

Title: Relief representation of the transport networks of the Atlantic Arc: distortions of space-time into "valleys" and "mountains"
Author: Alain L'Hostis
Abstract: The starting point for this work is the construction of a three-dimensional graph of the multimodal transport network. This structure is used to generate a space-time representation based on the average speeds of the transport modes. The speed differential creates space-time valleys that reveal "true proximities" and expose "false ones," to use Jacky Perreur's words. There are two construction methods: placing less efficient connections above or below the city plane. The comparison of these two methods is the subject of this paper.

Title: Modeling the relationships between agricultural activity and the territory: an attempt to predict the use of agricultural plots in twelve municipalities of Haute-Marne
Author: Pascal Thinon, Etienne Landais, Pascal Pierret, Christophe Perrot
Abstract: This paper presents a model for predicting the use of agricultural plots based on certain physical (slope, soil type, etc.) and geometric (size, shape) characteristics, their distance from the farm headquarters, and their classification as a specific type of farm. This model is part of the broader "MAP" (Modeling, Agriculture and Landscape) research program, currently underway at the SAD (Agricultural Systems and Development) unit of INRA Versailles. Some methodological choices are still being validated, and the results obtained are preliminary. The first part of this paper outlines the "MAP" program. The second part presents the agricultural land use prediction model developed for approximately 1,100 plots sampled in 12 municipalities in the Haute-Marne department.

Title: Land use and socio-economic structure: a study of the social dimension of the landscape
Author: Jean-Christophe Foltête
Abstract: Land cover, which represents the spatial interaction between natural and human systems, embodies a part of landscape production. Our study aims to highlight the relationships between municipal land cover composition and the underlying socio-economic structure in the Doubs department. A municipal land cover typology is constructed from the Corine Land Cover database using multiple correspondence analysis and classification. A statistical model is then fitted to predict the type of landscape present in a municipality based on its socio-economic characteristics. The technique used is discriminant factor analysis, with a more exploratory than decision-making focus.

Title: Spatial consequences of the "extended suburbanization" process: tools and methodologies for measuring them
Author: Xavier Duyck
Abstract: The process of "extended suburbanization" can be held responsible, by its very unfolding, for a series of consequences on the spatial and/or temporal distribution of the primary residences of "urban" populations on the outskirts of cities. A priori, different spatial distributions, referred to as "rurban," can be deduced depending on whether this dynamic location process operates in a homogeneous and isotropic environment or whether it takes place in a heterogeneous and/or anisotropic environment; these distributions can be quantitatively assessed in their differences using various tools and methodologies. Hypotheses can thus be formulated, and their comparison with empirical spatial distributions should allow us to test the validity of the process as well as to identify the characteristics of the environment in which it occurs.

Title: A grid method for determining road accessibility levels in rural areas: possibilities and constraints
Author: Sophie Passegué
Abstract: A raster-based geographic information system (IDRISI) is used to measure accessibility levels at an intra-municipal scale in a highly rural area (the countryside and hinterland of the middle Rhône). The approach is decidedly spatial, since the data model used is a priori better suited to the study of surfaces than to that of networks. However, the very limited nature of the information in this type of space establishes the areal as the essential organizing principle, precluding a network-based modeling of supply and demand locations and the spaces between them. Beyond simply rasterizing the network, developing a road roughness model and disaggregating the population are ways to enrich more traditional approaches to accessibility (graph theory) to facilities and offer numerous avenues for spatial analysis, understanding organizations, and land-use planning. Furthermore, pixels are no longer just elements of space but spatial units to which different statistical treatments can be applied.

Title: Accessibility to major transport infrastructure: analysis and modeling
Author: Laurent Chapelon
Abstract: The NOD software, developed at the CESA laboratory, was designed to assess the spatio-temporal impacts of projects modifying transport services (infrastructure, regulations, frequencies, timetables, etc.). Within this framework, a specific module has just been developed to test the accessibility criteria established by the French law on spatial planning and development. This law stipulates that by 2015, "no part of the continental metropolitan area shall be located more than 50 kilometers or 45 minutes by car from either a motorway or a dual carriageway expressway connected to the national network, or from a station served by the high-speed rail network." Our modeling principle, based on describing networks using weighted graphs, allowed us, after automatically determining nodal junctions and calculating optimal routes in terms of time and distance, to characterize each node according to: 1) the number and nature of the criteria met; 2) the surplus or deficit of accessibility relative to each criterion taken separately; 3) the functions provided by the major node closest to the nodes studied. The resulting accessibility maps show the intervention zones necessary to comply with the legal criteria, as well as any criteria defined by the model user. In this regard, a modification of the time threshold for accessibility to rapid transit infrastructure was simulated (tested with 30 and 60 minutes) to study the evolution of the intervention zones. The applications cover the entire French territory (518 nodes) and a specific focus on the Poitou-Charentes region (190 nodes).

Title: Is the gravity model a suitable tool for modeling telephone flows?
Author: Pascal Gillon
Abstract: The gravity model is one of the main tools used in spatial interaction to understand the movement of people or goods. Based on the respective masses of locations and the distance separating them, it allows for a fairly accurate reproduction of reality, thanks to the optimization of the exponent of the distance function and a weighting coefficient that represents the product of the two masses (simple gravity model). We therefore used this tool to model telephone traffic between French cities. However, it appears that it does not explicitly account for intervening opportunities or the threshold effect caused by pricing (continuous distance function). A new model was then created that takes into account pricing (discrete function) as well as intervening opportunities and incorporates a notion of call frequency.

Title: Diffusion of innovations and functioning of urban systems: a comparison between West Germany and France
Author: Sophie Baudet-Michel
Abstract: Several research studies have shown that, over the past few decades and within an increasingly prominent European context, there has been a growing trend towards metropolitanization. Furthermore, it appears that two main forms of organization can be identified within national urban networks: the Parisian-type organization, centralized and highly polarized, which fosters the development of hierarchical relationships, on the one hand; and the Rhine-type organization, a network-based structure that promotes the development of multiple cross-sectoral relationships between cities, on the other. Within this framework, the evolution of the spatial distribution of business services has been examined. Given that business services are part of a cycle of economic innovation (the information cycle) that has been spreading throughout national urban systems for several decades, and considering the strong tendency of this activity to adopt a metropolitan location, it is believed that this approach allows for the study of the dual dynamics of cities at both the national and European levels. Beyond the invariants of the diffusion of innovations, the question has been raised of the existence of a relationship between a particular form of urban system and the modalities of the diffusion of economic innovations.

Title: The border effect in spatial interaction models: economic exchanges in the Europe of fifteen since 1973
Author: Didier Robert
Abstract: The existence of boundaries between two spatial units generally results in a decrease in trade between these areas: this is known as the "border effect." The geographical analysis of the "border effect" relies on the construction of "spatial interaction" models that highlight the structure of trade. Once the effects of distance and the economic size of the areas studied have been isolated, it is possible to determine whether or not this "belonging effect" exists. Furthermore, it can be directly incorporated into a "geographical interaction" model that simultaneously defines the constraint of distance and the border effect. Using these methods, the study of economic exchanges between the fifteen countries that now form the European Union, from 1971 to 1994, provides a measure of the economic and political integration of this group. An original trade structure is observed at the beginning of this period, in which a set of privileged relationships linking the British Isles and Northern Europe mirrored the existing European Union of six member states. We also note the originality of the evolution of the structure of exchanges, as well as the gradual and expected disappearance of the "border effect" that existed at the beginning of the 70s.

Title: Public infrastructure and location of activities
Author: Sylvie Charlot
Abstract: This paper examines the links between public spending and the spatial distribution of economic activities. The focus is on regional location models. The first part is devoted to constructing a regional equilibrium model inspired by Krugman's model, incorporating public spending. Public capital is generated through a tax levied on national output. It is distributed exogenously between two regions. It is assumed that public capital influences the productivity of local firms. The introduction of a public sector alters the equilibrium conditions. The second part focuses on short-term equilibrium conditions and the distribution of industrial activities based on the spatial allocation of public capital.

Title: Does the construction of a motorway stimulate the territories it crosses and influence the behavior of stakeholders?
Author: Marie-Agnès Lanneaux
Abstract: The establishment of the A39 Motorway Observatory has enabled, and will continue to enable, the measurement and understanding of the effects of a major transport infrastructure on the organization and management of the areas it crosses. The objective of this paper is to present the main findings of the study conducted over three years (1993-1996). It shows that the construction of a motorway like the A39 leads to changes in the organization and management of the territory. However, these changes vary depending on the "receiving area" and the local stakeholders who implement planning and development strategies. Specific locations are favored; the development of certain areas is thus inextricably linked to the will and dynamism of a few key players.

Title: The role of space in the history of an exceptional territory, the Luberon
Author: Cécile Helle
Abstract: A cultural and media product, a hinterland revitalized and periodically colonized by the North, the Luberon has been operating for over forty years with a growing tourist influence. Variously dubbed a "summer refuge for trendy Parisians," an "annex of the 16th arrondissement," or a "new French Riviera without the sea," this spatial system, in its current state, bears little resemblance to the time when property could be acquired for next to nothing and when locals watched with amusement as a handful of artists moved into the old buildings they themselves had abandoned decades earlier. Over nearly half a century, a number of disruptive events, generating meaning and identity, have occurred and contributed to the desirability of this territory. Throughout this process, the Luberon, through its own unique characteristics, has asserted itself as a true agent of its own destiny.

Title: Territorial information and decision-making: institutional challenges and technological changes. Revision of the Urban Development Master Plan (SDAU) for the Grenoble urban region.
Author: Grégoire Feyt
Abstract: The proliferation of GIS within territorial institutions poses three major problems: - the necessary "systematization" and "codification" of the vision(s) of the territory that technicians are required to produce or manipulate; - the risk that this underlying movement tends to reinforce the "Balkanization" of territorial information instead of being used to enable the development of a synthetic and dynamic overview of a territory and its evolution; - the traditional gap that the introduction of new technologies reveals, at least initially, between specialists (the "analysts" and managers of the territory) and users (elected officials and citizens). The communication aims to present a project co-led by the Grenoble region urban planning agency, the joint association for the master plan and researchers, geographers or sociologists: to consider the development of the master plan as both a challenge and an opportunity to promote the establishment of an institutional partnership at the methodological and technical level with a view to developing a sustainable and reliable Territorial Information System at the service of consultation and territorial decision-making.

Title: Actor behaviors and territorial dynamics
Author: Cécile Tannier
Abstract: Our project aims to design a decision-making tool for urban planning, applicable to the location strategies of commercial businesses. It is based on modeling the interactions between stakeholders (decision-makers, groups of socio-economic agents) and their territory. Two key ideas underpin this project. The first is that space represents a specific type of actor, influencing the behavior of socio-economic agents and, in turn, being modified by them. The second is to integrate the reasoning of municipal teams (who are the decision-makers in urban planning) into the model, in order to obtain a tool that is truly usable by them.

Title: Implementation of a database for vehicle guidance in urban environments
Author: Christine Matoux-Lamberts
Abstract: The Paris Urban Planning Workshop's urban database possesses a significant collection of cartographic data. As a centralized and general-purpose tool, it is essential that it be redeployed towards decentralized mapping tools geared towards supporting decision-making within the territory. A "wired" database covering Paris and the three surrounding departments concentrates information on roads and streets. The database's content, collection and maintenance methods, as well as two applications, are discussed here: the use of data for in-vehicle navigation and geocoding.

Title: Landscape metrics: two specific indicators of relief for spatial planning
Author: Kamal Serrhini
Abstract: Landscape is attracting increasing interest from a wide range of stakeholders working in diverse fields. In planning and urban development, the implementation of new projects often leads to their simulation in order to understand the issues of integration and impact on the surrounding space. The aim of my research is to develop a method for quantifying landscape variations. These variations can be due to "natural" or anthropogenic factors. Within the framework of the "Third Théo Quant Meetings," we focused on modeling and studying spatial variations in relief. We developed a model that allows us, firstly, to represent any space in three dimensions in different ways and, secondly, to simulate the dispersal of people through percolation according to certain criteria (altitude, shortest route, etc.). The objective is to provide planning professionals with a decision-making tool for landscape considerations.

Title: A geographical approach to noise in urban space: the example of Besançon
Author: Hélèné Houot
Abstract: Noise, a quality of life element still relatively unexplored by geographers, is nonetheless an interesting concept for them insofar as it allows them to connect territory and networks in their analysis of the city. Based on the AFNOR definition of this concept, our research question consists of investigating the links between the physical and functional structure of an urban space and the noise produced within it. From this idea stem three lines of inquiry: - development of a model of disturbance potential according to geographical and acoustic situations, combining a knowledge-based system and a geographic information system; - analysis of noise generators and acoustic fields contained within the main types of built fabric; - creation of indicators (particularly population density) aimed at weighting disturbance potential within the framework of spatial planning.

Title: The whole/part logic: the scientific basis of a language used by geographers
Author: Georges Nicolas
Abstract: Periodically, geographers fragment into specializations linked to scientific developments and ideological fluctuations. Consequently, this fragmentation leads to attempts at reunification. In 1978-1980, at the beginning of the current phase of fragmentation, three axioms of geography (chorological, situational, and chronological) were proposed to replace Vidal de la Blache's unifying principles. The basic mechanism of the axioms, differentiation, was accurate, but the formulation of the chorological axiom was circular. This was reformulated as two chorological definitions of the object of geography, serving as the foundation for a logic. This logic is not yet another attempt to reunify geographies but a starting point for creating a language enabling communication between them. The other two axioms, which refer to principles not specific to geography, have been abandoned.

Title: Spatial analysis and geographical phenomena
Author: Jean-François Hangouët
Abstract: The term "spatial analysis" is vague in geography, but two complementary fields of practice help to define it more precisely: on the one hand, there is exploratory spatial analysis, which, as choromatics illustrates, involves questioning certain mysterious geographical data (what meaning do they have?); on the other hand, perhaps less intentional, although cartographic generalization provides an intensive example, there is constitutive spatial analysis, or the acceptance of data in their spatial arrangement (these signs are in cartographic relation). Both analyses are fruitful because the scientist, geographer, or cartographer, far from being content with the data, immediately senses through them what they represent of the real world, naturally taking them as manifestations of geographical phenomena. Their automation, however, is complicated by the fact that digital data evokes nothing for the computer and that their inadequacy (traces instead of forms, lists instead of distributions) distances them from the referents expected by the user. The geographical meaning of digital data, if not stored, can nevertheless be recalled from them thanks to the attitude of the researcher in geographical information science, an attitude which we describe here, from an epistemological point of view, under the name of phenomenology.

Title: Concepts for describing multi-representation databases
Author: Christelle Vangenot
Abstract: One of the major limitations of current spatial data models is their limited capacity to handle multiple representations of the same geographic objects from different viewpoints or at different levels of resolution. In this article, we first identify the needs arising from the presence of multiple representations of the same objects, then we propose concepts for associating several representations with an object, describing the validity of topological associations, linking corresponding objects at different resolutions, and finally, describing and querying objects and their attributes at different levels of semantic resolution.

Title: The systems approach as a tool for structuring spatio-temporal databases
Author: Marie-Hélène De Sède, Alexandre Moine
Abstract: Territories encompass spatio-temporal entities whose functioning relies on the relationships established between different categories of actors. However, the various databases that describe them poorly reflect this complexity, ultimately leading to the partial exploitation of a very rich informational potential. Thus, territorial data is often reduced to its graphic dimension alone, the harmonization of heterogeneous databases poses significant semantic and structural problems, and the results of their use are poorly sustained. Many of the identified problems originate from a lack of conceptualization upstream of the practical phases of use, during the modeling and structuring stages of the databases. The objective of this research is to propose a methodology for structuring spatio-temporal databases based on: - a systemic approach to conceptualizing the relationships between territorial entities and actors; - the proposal of a generic data hosting structure based on the upstream systemic approach and independent of downstream applications. - a modeling formalism integrating the spatio-temporal dimension of entities.

Title: MADS, or spatio-temporal information at the fingertips of its users
Author: Christine Parent, Esteban Zimanyi, Pier Donini, Corinne Plazanet, Stefano Spaccapietra, Christelle Vangenot
Abstract: Despite the recognized benefits of the conceptual approach to application modeling, existing spatiotemporal conceptual models do not meet the needs of designers. In this article, we briefly present the MADS model along three axes: structural concepts, spatial concepts, and temporal concepts. The orthogonality of the concepts allows for a model that is both simple (since these concepts are independent) and powerful (since the concepts can be freely combined). The model has been implemented, and translations exist into other operational models.

Title: The measurement of local indicators considered as a spatial bootstrap
Author: Jean-Christophe Foltête
Abstract: Our approach involves linking two seemingly unrelated techniques: bootstrapping and local indicators. Bootstrapping is a resampling method designed to observe the stability of any statistical measure; local indicator calculations consist of iterating a relationship calculation between variables by successively selecting the spatial neighborhood of the units studied. In both cases, the analysis is no longer based on a single model but on a large series of subsamples. From this perspective, local indicators serve to observe the spatial stability of any statistical measure. We attempt to demonstrate their value compared to a global model through a specific example: the relationship between population density and the daily mobility of the working population in Franche-Comté.

Title: From quantitative to qualitative, landscape decision-making
Author: Jacques Monnier-Raball
Abstract: The expression "landscape decision" seems common sense. However, it is not without its ambiguities. First, it suggests that one considers the current state of a given context without taking into account the more or less rapid evolution of the natural environment: one cannot therefore arbitrarily detach oneself from an ongoing process. Second, the expression suggests that the landscape finds its own end within itself. Finally, it assumes that any decision made within the environment entails predictable, probable, or even certain consequences, following a causal logic, that is, a purely linear chain of principles and effects, without considering its systemic nature as decisive: any action in space and time involves a certain number of uncertainties...

Title: Implementation of a territorial information system for estuaries: application to the mouth of the Seine
Author: Jean-Côme Bourcier
Abstract: This research proposes the implementation and operational use of a Geographic Information System (GIS) specific to the Seine estuary, using a multi-thematic geographic database. The objective is to design a territorial information system encompassing the diverse environmental aspects of the estuarine environment and exhibiting a transferable methodology. Within the framework of the national research program on wetlands, this system has demonstrated its effectiveness by improving the understanding of these areas through the relevant integration of geographic information.

Title: The SIGAUR project (Geographic Information System and Urban Acoustics): new perspectives for the spatial analysis of noise pollution
Author: Erwan Quesseveur
Abstract: This article presents a research project addressing the integration of a noise pollution information layer into a geographic information system. After discussing the current state of noise pollution and the methods currently in place to combat it, we will demonstrate the new perspectives offered for the spatial analysis of noise pollution. By comparing a territory's noise exposure to its vulnerability to noise, we aim to propose a spatially explicit decision-making criterion for land-use planning. This project is the result of a collaboration between the Scientific and Technical Center for Building (CSTB) and the geographic information system team at the Institute of Alpine Geography (Grenoble).

Title: Building your own maps: the development of interactive statistical tools integrated into a geographic information system
Author: Benoît Ogier
Abstract: Microcomputer operating systems today offer user-friendly interfaces. Furthermore, some geographic information systems (GIS) provide interesting development possibilities through plug-ins in the most common programming languages (Pascal, C, Delphi, etc.). Building on this foundation, we were able to enhance the functionalities of a GIS (spatial queries, route calculation, data management, mapping, etc.) with a series of statistical and graphical modules. These tools provide the user with all the statistical information and graphical representations necessary for a complete data analysis. Indeed, the modules are interconnected, allowing a study to be approached from multiple perspectives simultaneously and enabling comparison of the results of different methods. Moreover, the map is automatically updated as soon as data is categorized using one of the modules. We are therefore faced with complete interactivity between geographic information systems, maps, and statistics. But we can go further and consider experimenting with other graphic tools, particularly for processing the results of factor analyses.

Title: Image, learning, visual appropriation of space
Author: Robert Borodkine
Abstract: Imagery is a key element that accompanies the geographical approach in its many facets: legible landscapes, remote sensing, or more broadly, the spatial understanding of phenomena. From this perspective, automatic image processing is undeniably valuable, but despite its undeniable advantages, it does not yet fully rival human vision, whose adaptability remains unmatched. Therefore, we have undertaken research that places learning at the heart of image analysis. This research is conceived as a confrontation between cybernetic and geographical approaches, the latter being based on a relationship to space that takes into account its object-related, functional, and subjective dimensions. In particular, we have explored the concepts of representation and correlation in greater depth. This research leads to a model based on the notions of learnability and perceptual appropriation of the environment. This model sheds new light on the relationships we have with space, an object of sensory perception and mental structuring, but also on the very problem of modeling the system that constitutes the environment in its most global sense.

Title: The graph and the graphy of the Earth: a formal exercise to commemorate the bicentenary of the voyage to equatorial America
Author: Hervé Gazel
Abstract: This paper focuses on the migration of written geographical knowledge to a digital format. Such a migration can be conceived as hypertextualization. It involves examining the relationship between the graph and geographical writing. The example of climate classification, which draws on Humboldt's work, demonstrates how the transformation of geographical knowledge is linked to the analysis of the relationship between the graph and the written representation of the Earth.

Title: Taxonomy and remote sensing: the persistence of names during resolution changes
Author: Denise Blamont, Marcel Raffy
Abstract: The rules governing the relationship between radiometric nomenclature and changes in resolution are presented, along with a method for developing a low-resolution taxonomy from a high-resolution nomenclature. An example of mapping a Himalayan region using images of different resolutions illustrates this presentation.

Title: Field observations and remote sensing (King's Bay, Northwest Svalbard)
Author: Dominique Laffly
Abstract: Field observations are fundamental in remote sensing: depending on the study's purpose, the description of the observed landscapes will be more or less detailed. A simple identification of the main land cover features requires few indicators and does not necessitate precise location. In contrast, analyzing pixel content for statistical modeling relies on a detailed thematic description of very precisely located points. In this case, the images used must be correctly georeferenced, and location in the field is determined using differential GPS. The remaining challenges are selecting the points to analyze and observing their content. In this article, we present a method designed to address these two issues. Our approach is based on the technique of systematic non-aligned sampling. This technique allows us to consider both the luminance of the observed points and their location to define the sampling plan. The examples shown are from a study carried out on the sandurs of the Brøgger peninsula in northwestern Svalbard (SPOT XSP images).

Title: Use and evaluation of remote sensing in the study of urban development: the example of the Oran metropolitan area (Algeria)
Author: Nourredine Benabadji, Abdelkrim Benammar, Abed Bendjelid, Kheira Tabet Aoul
Abstract: The aim of this article is to examine how satellite image analysis can contribute to the study of urban growth in Algeria. We have observed that the city of Oran, Algeria's second largest city, exhibits areas of significant expansion (to the east and south); however, this often excessive growth has occurred without prior consideration for urban quality. This study comprises two parts: a) we begin by highlighting the scale of this often unplanned growth and the speed of its development, while identifying priority directions. This analysis is based on classifications performed on two multispectral satellite images (Spot XS 1986 and 1995); b) in a complementary study, currently underway, we attempt to make future projections regarding the evolution of this urban fringe and its capacity to accommodate redevelopment projects.

Title: Summer pasture landscapes: from remote sensing to synthetic mapping
Author: Muriel Harguindeguy
Abstract: In the Pyrenees, summer pastures are high-altitude grazing lands. Sensitive environments, undergoing rapid change, coveted and crucial to a fragile economy, they are receiving particular attention. In this context, a detailed understanding of these pastures is more necessary than ever to carry out relevant pastoral assessments. These assessments require maps of plant composition in relation to their pastoral value over large areas. The acquisition of this information can be facilitated by the use of remote sensing, which allows for the production of thematic land-use maps for applied purposes (maps of pastoral value, potential livestock density, etc.).

Title: Systematic analysis of the visible landscape from ground photographs: example of the Loven East basin, King's Bay, Svalbard
Author: Madeleine Griselin, Serge Ormaux
Abstract: Photographic sampling and systematic image analysis procedures were developed by geographers in Besançon based on several studies of temperate environments. This work presents an adaptation of the method to a primarily abiotic environment. In 1998, the landscapes of a partially glaciated basin in Svalbard (Loven East) were surveyed on a very large scale using a dual spatial and temporal sampling approach. The structure of the image database and the principles of its use are then described.

Title: Spatial concentration of road accidents: method for identifying black spots based on spatial autocorrelation, application and sensitivity analysis
Author: Benoït Flahaut
Abstract: The aim of this contribution is to identify areas of spatial concentration of road accidents in the form of black spots rather than black spots. Applying a geographical analysis method based on local measures of spatial autocorrelation allows us to locate these black spots. The relevance of the method is considered, and a study of the sensitivity of the results to different levels of contiguity and several weighting functions is presented. The results are also compared to those obtained using a kernel smoothing statistical method. Applying the method to a few roads demonstrates its suitability and applicability to the problem of locating black spots.

Title: Diagnosing road risk using a geographical approach: initial considerations
Author: Florence Huguenin-Richard
Abstract: Geographical analysis of road risk is a minor approach in accident analysis. However, considering space through the concepts of proximity, distance, and location should be able to reveal safety factors, particularly those related to the environment of the road accident. Currently, the development of spatial databases and their integration into geographic information systems are increasing. However, their exploitation requires the use of analytical methods adapted, on the one hand, to the nature and richness of the information and, on the other hand, to the problems of diagnosing and estimating road risk. Our study, conducted within the Lille metropolitan area, focuses on the problems of risk estimation using spatial methods: the problem of risk observation scales and data aggregation, the choice of risk estimators, and the integration of spatial characteristics as a safety factor.

Title: Surface representation of discrete point events: methodological comparison based on the distribution of road accidents in the urban community of Lille
Author: Arnaud Banos, Jérome Bolot
Abstract: Visually identifying spatial structures from a point cloud is a challenging task, especially when dealing with a large number of points. This article presents and compares two methods that significantly improve the graphical representation of spatial point data. The first method relies on a spatial grid, while the second is based on estimating a Kernel density function within moving windows.
