Both methods are applied to road traffic accidents in the Lille metropolitan area.

Title: Method for identifying local concentrations of events in a point cloud: application to road traffic accidents
Author: Arnaud Banos, Florence Huguenin-Richard
Abstract: This article presents an exploratory point cloud analysis method derived from Stan Openshaw's Geographic Analysis Machine (CAM). It allows for the automated identification of significant local concentrations of events within a given geographic space. As an example, the method is applied to road accidents that have occurred in the Lille metropolitan area.

Title: Network morphologies and accessibility
Author: Cyrille Genre-Grandpierre
Abstract: All our movements are constrained by the structure of transport networks. However, due to the unequal performance of these networks (spatial coverage, travel speed), they tend to make space non-homogeneous and non-isotropic, that is, non-Euclidean. Traditional geometry therefore seems increasingly inadequate for modeling space as it is experienced. Thus, in order to account for the changes in the interrelationships between places induced by these networks, we propose an analysis of their effects based on fractal geometry, which does not postulate the homogeneity of space and, consequently, provides a different framework for interpretation. We will first analyze the consequences of network structure in terms of spatial coverage, and then we will attempt to see how the quality of accessibility to a network of service providers depends on the morphology and functionalities of the network that connects these providers.

Title: Spatial analysis of rural exodus through the diffusion of surnames
Author: Sandrine Assalin
Abstract: For nearly two centuries, a massive rural exodus affected the hinterland of the middle Rhône Valley, generating a significant migratory flow from the countryside to the cities. While net migration has been the subject of numerous studies, the trajectories followed by migrants between the sending and receiving regions remain poorly understood. To reconstruct these trajectories, rare surnames originating from the hinterland are used as markers to track diffusion over a long period. The necessary surname information was collected from telephone directories, and the results were interpreted using a gravity model. The analysis reveals that while most migratory flows were directed towards the nearest major cities, as predicted by the model, specific spatial patterns are highlighted by the analysis of the model's residuals.

Title: Theoretical contribution to measuring the homogeneity of urban fabrics
Author: Mindjid Maïzia
Abstract: The study examines the city from the perspective of its built environment, its planimetric and volumetric form, its land use configuration, its plot divisions, its architecture, and so on. The aim is to quantify the internal morphological homogeneity that characterizes any urban fabric. The proposed analytical method involves decomposing the city into systems of semantically identified elements. The set of these systems is called a meta-system and corresponds to the entire coverage of a GIS. Through two indicators, morphological deviation and the irregularity rate (differential), it is possible to measure the degree of regularity of a given morphology.

Title: The resilience of a spatial system: the example of the Comtat
Author: Christine Aschan-Leygonie
Abstract: The concept of resilience originates in physics and was subsequently transferred to ecology. Currently, in ecology, resilience is understood as the capacity of a system to integrate a disturbance into its functioning without altering its qualitative structure. The degree of resilience of a system in relation to a disruptive event does not in any way prejudge its return to its previous state after a disturbance. It implies that the system manages to integrate the disturbance, or even benefit from it, and thus improve its functioning. This study applies this concept to geography through a case study: the dynamics of the Comtat Venaissin spatial system during two periods of disruption: the agricultural crises of the second half of the 19th century and recent economic difficulties. The new European landscape has indeed placed Comtat Venaissin agriculture at a disadvantage compared to more competitive rivals. In order to highlight the various criteria that influence the degree of resilience of a spatial system, a qualitative formalization in different dynamic phases was carried out.

Title: Urban complexity and the measurement of risk
Author: Lorena Franzini, Lidia Diappi
Abstract: This research analyzes the concept of risk and develops a potential tool for studying urban systems. The assessment and management of territorial risks have been extensively explored in detail by numerous contributions, particularly those concerning the role of spatial planning in prevention strategies. In an urban setting, the approach differs when the damaging event is not accidental but structural, and the risk is directly linked to the behavior of social systems. This paper considers the subject from an analytical perspective, aiming to develop an investigative tool capable of accounting for the multidimensional nature of the phenomena that generate risk and the complex nature of risk itself. Risk analysis can reasonably be included in the debate surrounding vulnerability, given the crucial importance of aspects such as prevention and security in urban environments. This paper proposes an answer to the questions raised by these key aspects of risk, attempting to move beyond the traditional approach to risk analysis based on additive and compensatory logics. Two applications are proposed: a micro-scale investigation aimed at determining the relationships between urban morphology and air pollution caused by automobiles and an urban-scale study for the construction of an analytical-descriptive structure of the risk conditions generated by the simultaneous presence of different critical factors.

Title: Towards the end of industrial suburbs?
Author: Edwige Dubos-Paillard, Patrice Langlois
Abstract: This article presents the evolution of industrial locations within the Rouen agglomeration from 1976 to 1992. It relies on several statistical indicators which highlight a spatial dispersion of the sector of activity linked to the decrease in the number of establishments and employees during the period, but also to the appropriation of new sites by a certain category of industry.

Title: A simulation model of internal migration in the Basilicata region (Italy)
Author: Nicola Tamma
Abstract: This work presents a gravity model, proposing a formulation that follows in the footsteps of potential models, according to which the difference in opportunities offered in each center of the study area constitutes a measure that determines the aptitude for emigration between the municipalities of the Basilicata region. This application is proposed to reconstruct and interpret migratory flows, thus contributing to the explanation of the regional dynamics of Basilicata, which are typical of an inland region of the Apennines in southern Italy, where the complex morphology of the territory becomes a factor with evident effects. The model formulation presents innovative aspects, particularly in the calibration and selection procedure for the variables studied in the analytical phase of the research.

Title: A methodology to investigate the effects of globalization on local territorial structures
Author: Silvana Lombardo, Luisa Santini
Abstract: The main objective of this study is to identify the existence and influence of economic changes on territorial organization at the global level, in terms of the organization of production systems and location choices. Few studies have been conducted in this area, undoubtedly due to insufficient data and the specific nature of the numerous local territorial systems. This observation led us to propose a methodology capable of enriching knowledge in this field. The work focused on: • theoretical aspects relating to new models of territorial organization, such as the network paradigm, the impact of economic globalization on production systems, and internationalization; • empirical aspects through the analysis of production systems in two Italian regions (Lazio and Abruzzo), which have been little studied but for which recent developments have shown profound changes, particularly at the level of small and medium-sized enterprises, with local systems adapting to the adjustments brought about by the evolution of the global economic system. These two cases were analyzed using a questionnaire sent to a sample of companies. Due to the new confidentiality law severely restricting the use of many sources, the research relied primarily on data provided by major official bodies (the Central Institute of Statistics and the Union of Chambers of Commerce). A number of indicators were identified in order to: • provide data for the cases studied, • simplify the statistical scope and extract the sample. Ultimately, the questionnaire made it possible to identify the general characteristics of the companies, the relationships in which they are involved, and to identify and assess the relevance of location factors.

Title: The effects of the national road network on departmental economic development in France: a modeling approach
Author: Bernard Fritsch
Abstract: This article adopts a model-based approach, aiming to assess the extent to which the hypothesis that the national road network is a factor in departmental economic development is empirically valid, and to measure its economic effects. It relies on the estimation, through multiple regression analyses, of the coefficients of mathematical models of the aggregate production function type, based on departmental observations. The results show that market GDP and the productivity of market activities depend significantly on the level of road and highway infrastructure; that disparities in levels of economic development are well explained by departmental road allocations; and that, all other things being equal, an increase in these allocations translates into increased economic activity. These effects of the national road network appear more pronounced in departments with low or medium population and economic activity densities.

Title: Towards a model of home-to-work travel and associated travel
Author: Jean Renaud Dumas, Sophiz Passegué, Mohamed Hilal
Abstract: The separation of place of residence from place of work (employment, shops, services, etc.) serves as the basis for the creation of functional zones such as urban areas, employment zones, or catchment areas. Commuting patterns indicate an increasing concentration of jobs, shops, and services in cities and a residential dispersion around them. This work attempts to situate the logic of inter-municipal travel in different spatial categories (urban and rural) by exploring, in particular, how several travel motives can be combined during the same sequence. The main hypothesis is that there are primary drivers of travel (all those related to employment) onto which travel with secondary motives is grafted. The main data source used is the 1993-1994 IN RETS-INSEE transport and communications survey, which will be matched with data from the general population census and the municipal inventory.

Title: Intermunicipal cooperation and territory: a first systemic approach
Author: Florence Vaivre
Abstract: Intermunicipal cooperation takes extremely varied forms depending on the local context. This study aims to assess the capacity of this form of cooperation to develop genuine territorial integration. This objective notably involves identifying local factors likely to have an influence and then the local system that integrates them.

Title: Urban form and distribution of pollutants
Author: Christiane Weber
Abstract: Air pollution, which characterizes our cities, is of increasing interest to scientists, as well as political and administrative actors and the general public. The proportion of city dwellers exposed to this type of pollution is steadily growing across the European continent, leading European and national directives to attempt to regulate its causes by increasing the means of prevention (industrial and technical, but also administrative and legal), as well as alert and communication measures. However, to ensure the success of these initiatives, it is necessary to address these phenomena with a more comprehensive approach than has been used until now. While models of air pollutant distribution have been well developed at macroscopic scales, the urban scale is much less so. The research project presented here adopts such an approach, linking the microscopic scale of observation (the monitoring station) to a larger scale (the urban area). The main hypothesis is that urban forms have a significant impact on the distribution of pollutants, whether at the street level, the measurement site level, or the city-wide level. Furthermore, to compensate for the insufficient number of measurement stations, it is necessary to find ways to spatially represent the collected data in order to obtain a comprehensive picture of air pollution phenomena. Satellite imagery is used here as an information vector, providing a solution to this problem.

Title: Space, entropy, environment
Author: Michel Phipps
Abstract: The advent of individual-based modeling and the development of geographic information systems have sparked renewed interest in the geographic applications of information theory. An algorithm designed for the analysis of spatial distributions with discrete variables is presented. It consists of progressively reducing the entropy of the system using information provided by a combination of variables describing the system. The results of this approach reveal a redundancy that measures the level of order of the system. An application to the distribution of forest cover types in Manitoba, Canada, is presented.

Title: An analysis of the evolution of intra- and inter-regional contrasts using mathematical morphology: The example of Provence-Alpes-Côte d'Azur
Author: Sylvie Autiero
Abstract: The approach presented here has two objectives. Firstly, it highlights intra- and inter-regional divisions and their evolution within a territory. Secondly, it reveals the areas experiencing the most significant changes over a given period. The search for contrasts between places and their spatio-temporal analysis is facilitated by the use of mathematical morphology. Indeed, the application of this methodology in detecting existing discontinuities allows for the simultaneous consideration of the layout of places and their value, while also enabling an "in situ" visualization of the results. We have chosen to work with variations in population density to account for the intensity of the divisions produced over time by population movements. The demonstration will be based on the Provence-Alpes-Côte d'Azur region, an area where the situations encountered are numerous and complex.

Title: Boundaries, packing and diversity. Spatial scaling laws in squatter settlements
Author: Fabiano Sobreira, Marcelo Gomes
Abstract: The geometry of squatter settlements on the northeastern coast of Brazil is examined and compared to settlements in the central region of Kenya. In particular, the fragmented structures of the islands of habitations in these settlements, and the void area (regions unoccupied by houses) are studied. We find that such settlements, when constrained by urban and natural boundaries, present robust configurational patterns, expressed by statistical distributions with scaling properties. Such scaling properties, when considered in planning purposes, can be useful on describing and predicting the spatial and social parameters of such squatter settlements. Several scaling functions and other mathematical expressions, which are of interest in urban studies, are also derived and discussed.

Title: Radial analysis of the urban fabric of Oran
Author: Sadika Selka, Abdel Benhamar
Abstract: This article presents radial analysis, a fractal method for analyzing urban fabrics. Applied to the urban fabric of Oran, a city experiencing rapid urban expansion due to various factors, this analysis supports studies conducted by researchers, including P. Frankhauser, on major cities and metropolises worldwide. For this analysis, a satellite image was used instead of a cartographic map, as was the case for applications to other urban fabrics.

Title: Changes in the location of French industry from 1990 to 1995. A counting model approach
Author: Jean-Marc Zaninetti
Abstract: Industrial geography evolves primarily due to the creation and closure of establishments. The distribution of these events depends on structural factors, such as whether a company belongs to a group or not, and its business lines. It also depends on purely spatial effects, such as agglomeration strength and regional effects. It is this latter effect that we seek to isolate using a counting model. The number of events follows a heterogeneous Poisson process. The model calculates the differential probabilities associated with the various local combinations of factors. The spatial distribution of the regional effect contrasts the Northeast of the country, where changes are slow, with the Southwest and the Paris region, where industrial organization is evolving rapidly. The Northwest regions realize the main benefits, while the Southeast is in line with the national average.

Title: Methods for evaluating regional training policies in France. How is the spatial dimension of the phenomena studied taken into account?
Author: Patrice Caro
Abstract: The five-year law of December 1993 concerning labor, employment, and vocational training granted new powers to the 26 French regions in the area of training. This law mandates an evaluation of the impact of regional vocational training policies every three years (Article 53). Following two evaluation phases (1993-1996 and 1996-1999), a third phase is currently being prepared, aiming to assess the impact of regional policies on equal opportunities for young people in accessing training and employment. The evaluation methods used are almost identical for each phase, relying on quantitative and qualitative analyses of regional and sub-regional situations. The evaluation work resulted in the production of three types of materials: regional statistical portraits, synthesis studies resulting from interview surveys in the 26 regions, and a general technical report. This article will focus on showing the methodological choices that guide these evaluations among the results obtained and published, and how the spatial dimension of the phenomena studied is taken into account by the actors in the regions and by the authors of the evaluation (diversity of labor markets, location of initial and continuing training schemes, geographical mobility of young people, etc.).

Title: The benefits of sustainable management of aquatic environments for the purpose of enhancing the value of territories through recreational fishing
Author: Raphaël Berthold
Abstract: Recreational fishing encompasses the three pillars of sustainable development, presenting significant ecological and socio-economic challenges. We propose to demonstrate the numerous benefits of its implementation by comparing the attractiveness (to anglers) of several fishing areas with varying water quality and fish populations. These conditions may reflect the ecological evolution of waterways, but they are also the result of human interventions with diverse consequences. We will therefore show how humans can influence environments and, consequently, the presence or absence of species of high heritage value, and how these two factors affect the intensity of recreational fishing.

Title: Analysis of centralized spatial diffusion processes: The case of service establishments providing services to businesses
Author: Eric Daudé
Abstract: This article presents an analysis of the expansion patterns of business service networks in France. The growth of a business network is expressed by the multiplication of the number of establishments managed by a head office. While a wide variety of growth objectives and numerous location factors can be observed by company and sector, the objective of this article is to identify recurring patterns in location strategies at a global level. Are the relocation patterns of establishments from their head offices comparable to the spatial diffusion processes of innovations? Contiguity matrices and the hierarchy of employment zones are used to analyze the diffusion of establishments controlled by their head offices. Results at the global level allow us to understand the influence of diffusion processes through contagion and hierarchical channels on the expansion patterns of business service networks. At the local level, a strong impact of the degree of centrality of the head office's location on the spatial distribution of its establishments is observed.

Title: Modeling and simulation of flood risk in a Mediterranean urban environment
Author: Damienne Provitolo
Abstract: A new object of research in the scientific world, risk—whether of natural, technological, economic, or health origin—continues to worry society. In this paper, we focus on a crucial aspect of risk: its complexity, as it combines hazard and vulnerability. Dynamic system modeling allows us to grasp this complexity and is therefore used to construct risk models. This methodology not only integrates the vulnerability component into the risk system but also transcends the divide between nature and society. Above all, it offers the possibility of moving beyond a static view of phenomena to study them as dynamic systems. In this context, the STELLA 5.1 Research software is used to model and simulate all the stock and flow equations related to the risk system.

Title: Optimization of locating problems in urban contexts
Author: Roberto de Lotto
Abstract: The object of the paper is the analysis of a location-like problem with reference to an urban context. The uncapacitated and capacitated urban functions and facilities are considered. This kind of problem is usually stated as follows: given m clients and n potential sites for locating prespecified functions and facilities select an optimal set of locations. The paper formulates a traffic network model oriented to the analysis, simulation and sub-optimal solution to a location-like problem. The model is analogous as it describes the road network as an electric network; it describes each lane of a road as an oriented link, characterized by (time-varying) parameters, such as the route time at given unsaturated conditions. Road intersections are represented as nodes with inflows and outflows. The effect of the location of a facility or a function in a precise site over the surrounding extended area is particularly modeled. The proposed model is based on an interactive software package, as a decision support system, supported by a graphical front-end named ULISSE, on LINUX platform, which shows the plan of the selected city, and that allows to show the result of the simulation with the possibility to change each parameter of the net directly on a friendly graphical front end. The main result is the optimized location of the facilities or functions in the urban context, visualized directly on the city plan. Other results are: -the influence area of each service site; -the degree of use of each service; -the induced traffic flow increment on each road; -the total cost of any given service location. Moreover other results can be obtained: -the minimum path matrix for all the nodes of the network; -the distribution of traffic due to a given origin-destination matrix.

Title: Factors influencing the growth of residential areas in peri-urban zones. An attempt at integration applied to the Namur region (Belgium) using cellular automata.
Author: Jehan Decrop
Abstract: The phenomenon of urban sprawl is one of the most significant geographical processes affecting mixed urban-rural areas in Western Europe over the past few decades. While a substantial body of literature has highlighted the numerous factors responsible for this phenomenon, integrating them into a spatio-temporal model remains far more challenging given the complexity of the processes involved. This article proposes a methodology for modeling the growth of residential areas based on the principles of cellular automata. By combining a quantitative module focusing on the temporal dynamics of the number of households with a spatial module of potential location factors, this model could lead to prospective simulations of residential area growth. The application area for this model is the urban region of Namur (Belgium). This article does not claim to be exhaustive and only addresses the methodological aspects of an ongoing doctoral thesis.

Title: Self organized maps: a neural clustering method for urban analysis
Author: Lorena Franzini, Paola Bolchi, Lidia Diappi
Abstract: This research focuses on experimenting with a data processing method based on Neural Networks, and therefore on a connectionist cognitive approach. The aim is to explore the relationship structure between urban indicators and to understand the structural links within urban systems. The study analyzed the connections present in a set of variables for the city of Milan, divided into 144 statistical zones. The Milan database was analyzed using a definition of urban sustainability, interpreted as a positive interaction between the social, economic, and environmental systems, and to determine a series of indicators to express the relationships between these three systems. Previously, the same database had already been analyzed using a risk measurement methodology based on a threshold approach and Self-Associated Neural Networks. This paper presents a new version of Self-Organizing Maps (SOMs). SOMs implement a spatial organization process whereby input units are classified according to their urban characteristics. The network logically divides the input space into "clusters," where the principal components that differentiate the input data prevail. SOMs are networks that evolve through unsupervised and self-organizing learning, operating the input units in competition according to a "winner unit" principle. Applying this network typology allows the construction of Milan maps while maintaining spatial disaggregation into statistical zones. The results of SOMs have enabled the creation of "clustering" plans where zones are identified either by their high similarities or by their position in the output matrix (whose dimension must be defined at the beginning of the neural process).

Title: Spatial dynamics simulation. The example of population densification around Avignon
Author: Philippe Ellerkamp
Abstract: In the Avignon region, the spatial organization of population densities appears to strongly determine the spatial dynamics of settlement between 1936 and 1999. It seems possible to account for a significant portion of these dynamics using principles of dependence on the previous situation and interaction between neighboring spatial units. To verify the validity of these hypotheses, a simulation model was constructed. This model is a cellular automaton in which the cells have a resolution of one square kilometer. The model's operation is based on a local evolution rule that integrates a process of cell population diffusion and a process of population growth through external input. No global constraints or exogenous rules act on the cell dynamics. Only the initial configuration, which is the grid of densities from 1936 and represents the memory of the system's previous evolution, locally constrains the dynamics. This model does not claim to reproduce reality as observed on density maps; rather, it contributes to the search for fundamental spatial processes. The simulations demonstrate how very simple local mechanisms can generate coherent macro-dynamics. Existing configurations are thus amplified through both an increase in the polarization of the most heavily urbanized areas and a homogenization of peri-urban spaces through diffusion.

Title: Modeling urban sprawl: The case of Tijuana in Mexico
Author: Michel Le Page
Abstract: This article proposes three approaches to modeling urban expansion, using Tijuana, Mexico, as a case study. First, empirical observation of the structure, functions, and evolution of the urban system leads to an initial mapping. Second, a statistical method is developed based on two key components: the attraction of the urban center and the localized effect of topography. The third technique involves the use of a cellular automaton.

Title: Minor technological risk: localized database and visualization. The example of service stations in the Strasbourg urban community
Author: Claire Hiegel
Abstract: This article presents, through the example of service stations in the Strasbourg Urban Community, the development of an interactive tool to assist in responding to "minor" technological risks. Visualizing these risks makes them perceptible and tangible in space, and provides a comprehensive rather than fragmented view. The implementation of this tool required prior in-depth analysis of the relevant variables and criteria related to both hazards and vulnerabilities, in order to build a database tailored to minor technological risks.

Title: Ecology and GIS: a heritage management tool applied to natural tourist areas
Author: Jean-Christophe Loubier
Abstract: In a sustainable development approach, we have attempted to design a software management tool for local authorities. This set of interconnected software programs forms a meta-system that spatially represents the dynamics of the natural environment using Shannon's entropy equation. This allows fragile areas to be visualized in map form. Planners can thus quickly identify areas where the exploitation of the natural environment risks triggering serious, even irreversible, degradation. They can then prevent future development problems rather than simply addressing the consequences.

Title: Giving non-motorized modes of transport a chance through the development of road networks
Author: Cyrille Genre-Grandpierre
Abstract: The article begins by demonstrating how modern road networks, through the geography of accessibility imposed by their morphology, tend to structurally favor car use at the expense of active transportation modes. It then puts forward proposals for road network design that provide accessible and accessible routes for active transportation, illustrating the extent to which it is possible to combat car dependency for short-distance journeys.

Title: Geographic origin of the urban population
Author: Sandrine Assalin
Abstract: For approximately two centuries, rural populations have migrated to cities. This demographic concentration has followed a diffusion pattern from the countryside, resulting in a mixing of populations within urban areas. Cities have exerted varying degrees of attraction depending on their location and size. This study will focus on the central municipalities of medium-sized cities. This attraction can be measured through the diffusion of rare surnames, which serve as markers for tracking populations over long periods. This presentation will focus on the development of an experimental method for detecting population flows through the diffusion of rare surnames and the use of the chi-square test.

Title: Relevance of a method for analyzing spatial dynamics by taking into account road traffic flows
Author: Rémi Tauleigne
Abstract: This reflection stems from the lack of theoretical and methodological convergence between researchers interested in network analysis and those interested in spatial dynamics in human geography. Network morphology and flows, however, appear to play a significant role in structuring space and would therefore be essential to understanding spatial dynamics. This lack of convergence, which may only be apparent, seems largely linked to the difference in the nature of the variables used, since network variables are by nature "reticular" and most variables commonly used in spatial analysis are "area-based." This contribution thus emphasizes methodological aspects. In particular, it presents a method for comparing variables of different natures, such as road traffic flows and demographic variables, and evaluates its relevance for analyzing spatial dynamics.

Title: Disaggregated analysis: a luxury or a necessity? Application to the analysis of urban-scale travel generators
Author: Thomas Thévenin
Abstract: The disaggregated approach is too often neglected when analyzing travel generators at the urban scale. Yet, travel generators are key drivers of movement in urban life. Workplaces, shopping centers, and leisure venues attract and generate travel daily. It is therefore essential to pinpoint their precise locations and identify their characteristics in order to improve transportation networks. The objective of this article is to present a disaggregated analysis method for travel generators at the urban scale. To this end, the main principles of the disaggregated approach will be presented first. Next, the structure of the geographic information system will be detailed. Finally, the methods developed above will be illustrated with an application example: the optimal location of stations on a tram line currently under study in Besançon.

Title: Modeling visitor movement in natural areas. Evaluating the potential impacts of a development project.
Author: Fabrice Decoupigny
Abstract: A quick review of visitor movement patterns in natural areas reveals that tourist sites are increasingly frequented by local populations, particularly urban dwellers. A major problem is that these visitor flows are not integrated into traditional studies based on purely tourism-related indicators (number of overnight stays, tourist function, etc.). Drawing on observations made during visitor surveys, we developed a simulation model of visitor movement in a regional natural area (the FRED model). The model's challenge lies in formalizing two types of movement at two scales: car travel and pedestrian travel.

Title: The urban place-object, a morphogenetic singularity
Author: Sébastien Gadal
Abstract: The images transmitted by satellite represent matrices of electromagnetic pulses of portions of geographic space: pixels. These representations are neither the geographic objects themselves, nor their direct reflections in the form of reflected radiation. They are located on the screen using a geodetic coordinate system. We see localized differences between images. These differences are considered geographic because they are located on the Earth's surface. But is location sufficient to justify the label "geographic"? The question arises because several objects can be located in the same area. The geographic character, therefore, does not depend on location but on geographic differentiation. In the case of the morphogenetic modeling method of geographic space, we observe images of objects whose reflections are combined. Or, more precisely, differences between the images of objects which, most of the time, are not simple but combined, and for which, for example, urbanized areas are morphogenetic outgrowths. The morphogenetic method therefore relies not only on the geodetic differentiation of locations but also on the geographical differentiation of objects. All objects are considered to have a place on the Earth's surface. This method detects localized places before localized objects; that is, it seeks to represent geographical object-places.

Title: From the overall observation of changes in societies and rural areas
Author: Nathalie Fer
Abstract: This article presents the method initially developed for the study of wasteland in the Pays d'Auge (Normandy).

Title: From spatial memory, or learning
Author: Robert Borodkine
Abstract: The study of systems involving living organisms, with or without an anthropogenic component, and the concepts of ecosystem, geosystem, and metabolism, place great emphasis on the exchange and transformation of matter and energy. The information involved is often neglected. In this article, we propose considering the functioning of systems including living elements as being based on the information they contain rather than on the concepts of matter and energy. From this perspective, it is crucial to recognize that the quantitative approach—even when combined with a systems perspective—is not, in itself, a guarantee of objectivity: we are limited to considering only a portion of the inexhaustible mass of objective elements we could consider, which amounts to privileging certain aspects at the expense of others. We can then introduce the concepts of learning and sustained perception. These issues stem both from the non-random nature of properties that can be discovered within the environment, and from the way in which the environment can reveal them. This leads us to revisit a wide range of problems. Examples include the concept of an ecosystem's absorption capacity in the face of disturbances, the dynamics of such systems, certain indirect transformations of living organisms, the evolution of sensitivities and practices in relation to space and tools, and biodiversity.

Title: Geographical distance
Author: Georges Nicolas
Abstract: On a map, the distance between two points A and B is equal to the distance from A to B. On the ground, this is not the case. For someone walking, the effort required to climb from point A at the bottom of a mountain to point B at the summit is not equal to the effort required to descend it. This lack of symmetry, or non-reciprocity, is found in many other areas: economic, social, political, etc. The idea developed is that there is something common to all these distances: geographical distance. This is calculated using: 1) the geodetic distance dK, which is the sum of the lengths measured on the Earth's surface, using the metric system, between the locations of objects at A and B; 2) the numerical value of the objects located at A and B. It is measured by the product of the square root of the ratio between the numerical value of the objects and the square root of the geodetic distance that separates them.

Title: An experiment in analyzing textual data about household waste: advantages and conditions for using a method
Author: Estelle Kah
Abstract: Starting with the problem of a population's relationship with its environment in the context of household waste, this study examines the contributions of textual data analysis to define its advantages and limitations in a geographical survey. The method used, ALCESTE, is undoubtedly one of the most sophisticated and objective. An exploratory method that allows for the characterization and classification of speakers and their discourse based on geographical, social, or economic criteria, it can serve as a preliminary survey or confirmatory analysis. In behavioral analyses, particularly in relatively unexplored fields such as waste management, it allows for the definition of lexical contexts, paving the way for the development of evaluative propositions. It enables the interpretation of contradictions or the explanation of limitations within the survey itself. However, its strengths are accompanied by cumbersome aspects, difficulties in interpretation, and limitations inherent to its very nature.

Title: Waste transport. Method for assessing combinable potential: application to the case of Franche-Comté.
Author: Geoffroy Brischoux
Abstract: Over the past decade, numerous transport innovations have been developed, but none have truly progressed beyond the experimental stage. This article aims to assess the development potential of a new combined rail-road transport concept for household waste, using the example of waste produced in the Franche-Comté region. It will analyze, using several combination criteria, whether this alternative represents a significant strategic niche for the specific transport needs arising from the treatment of household and similar waste.

Title: Behind the regional disparities in GDP per capita in the European Union: Statistical analysis
Author: Laure Charleux
Abstract: This article presents a spatial statistical analysis of regional disparities in GDP per capita, a key indicator of the European Union's regional policy. The analysis unfolds in three stages, following a conventional three-step process: univariate analysis, linear regression modeling, and classification based on the variables selected by the regression. In conclusion, an assessment of eligibility for Objective 1 is carried out using the same variables.

Title: Young delinquents and statistics: The problem of classification in the interpretation of statistics on delinquency and urban violence.
Author: Veronica Noseda
Abstract: The interpretation of statistics on trends in crime and “urban violence” has been the subject of much debate among criminologists and sociologists. According to these researchers, the main bias in these statistics lies in the fact that they measure not the activity of offenders, but rather that of the police and other law enforcement agencies. Few researchers, however, have examined the problem of the classification categories used in these statistics and their social applications. In this article, we will attempt to demonstrate that a circular relationship may exist between certain categories of social and territorial division used in the statistics and the activity of law enforcement agencies.

Title: Evaluation process in home car parking. Vague formalization of the level of acceptance by motorists of a restrictive parking management policy.
Author: François Pezzoli
Abstract: Since the 1980s, parking problems have intensified significantly. Initial models have evolved, and new ones have been created to aid decision-making. Depending on the objectives and context, different models can address common goals; therefore, we classified them according to whether they were descriptive or explanatory, and then according to whether they were related to user behavior or to parking availability and the traffic network. Our work is unique in that it focuses specifically and exclusively on city center residents. Constantly exposed to problems of cost, security, and a lack of nearby parking spaces, these drivers consider their parking space an extension of their home. It is therefore assumed that they have a preferred parking spot, deemed acceptable by the individual who occupies it. To measure the resident's trade-offs in their parking strategy, we used a method that incorporates the concepts of satisfaction trade-offs and compensatory phenomena. It allows us to nuance Boolean logic and to observe in detail how an individual behaves in the transition from accepting a proposition to its total rejection.

Title: The usefulness of high-resolution images for assessing the role of vegetation in urban planning. What resolution for which needs?
Author: Anne Puissant, Christiane Weber
Abstract: Population growth in Europe and worldwide is impacting the quality of our environment: air pollution, noise pollution, and traffic congestion are concerns for individuals and especially for land managers. In this context, the development of environmental indicators is essential to assess the impact of green spaces on urban nuisances. This article presents the results of a quantitative analysis based on the automatic extraction of land cover classes from simulated images at different resolutions (10 to 1 m) of the Strasbourg metropolitan area. The objective is to define a user-oriented typology and to determine the appropriate spatial resolution for identifying descriptive variables of environmental quality (solely in terms of land cover).

Title: Dynamic indicators for monitoring mudflats in the Seine estuary
Author: Thomas Pouchin
Abstract: In the Seine estuary, the areas of bare mudflats have decreased considerably in just a few decades. While sedimentation is a natural phenomenon here, its scale is excessive and particularly worrying, as mudflats are vital habitats for migratory birds and primary feeding grounds. The degradation and transformation of these rich and specific biotopes is one of the phenomena that necessitated the establishment of a wetland observatory in the Seine estuary. The analysis of a time series (1979 to 2000) composed of satellite images and aerial photographs has allowed for a detailed and consistent understanding of the landscape dynamics of this sensitive area. After identifying the main spatial changes, quantifying the movements (in terms of surface area) has enabled the development of trends that provide information on the speed of these phenomena and their future dynamics. In addition to sedimentation, a significant process of estuary artificialization, which multiplies direct and indirect environmental impacts on the integrity of biotopes, has been studied. The main result of this research is a precise and comprehensive synopsis of the spatial changes that have occurred in these mudflat areas. In the Seine estuary, the 21st century is beginning with the construction of the gigantic "Port 2000" port terminal. Its impact on the estuary's natural environments is largely unknown, making the wetland observatory more relevant than ever.

Title: The consequences of El Niño/La Niña events in the Sinú watershed
Author: Rigaud Sanabria
Abstract: Given that the water and climate regime of the Sinú (Colombia) is disrupted by ENSO/LNSO events, we attempted to determine the spatio-temporal interaction of these phenomena on rainfall and river flows. We began with two questions: What is the spatial distribution of the consequences of these events? And, furthermore, can we predict the season, duration, and water balances of future events? In the Sinú, rainfall deficits and severe droughts are observed during El Niño, and abundant rainfall occurs during La Niña. Floods with catastrophic consequences occur during La Niña, as in August 1988, when nearly 69,000 hectares were affected. During the 1997–1998 El Niño, rainfall decreased by 50% and river flows by 40%.

Title: The geometries of the body. Socio-spatial diffusion and ideal types of karate practice: an attempt at modeling
Author: Ludovic Jeanne
Abstract: This article presents the application—within the framework of a social geography problem—of the so-called "ideal-typical" method initiated by Max Weber. The research focused on analyzing the socio-spatial diffusion of bodily practices, and more specifically, that of karate throughout the world. From this question emerged a problem centered on examining the interaction between the socio-spatial process of diffusion and the object of diffusion. Such a problem, by hypothesis, attributes the transformation of the practice and the variability of its modalities, in time and space, to the diffusion process itself. Consequently, the ability to develop ideal types of karate practice is a direct contribution to the interpretation and understanding of the diffusion process, helping to overcome the real complexity of the object and the social world associated with it. A model was constructed based on three ideal types of karate practice. This model allows us to interpret the effects of socio-spatial diffusion on disseminated practice in simple terms. Despite this simplicity, it raises fundamental questions about the nature of diffusion phenomena and their effects. Indirectly, this model gives social and corporeal substance to a socio-spatial process that could, at least theoretically, have been analyzed solely from a spatial perspective. The application of this "Weberian" method raises two epistemological questions, which are examined here: interdisciplinarity and the relationship between an ideal-typical model and reality.

Title: Modeling sociocultural communication networks in the city. Example of the city of Latakia (Syria)
Author: Ossama Khadour
Abstract: This article presents the design and implementation of a computer tool for representing, calculating, and analyzing a communication network derived from a territorial projection of the sociocultural system. A theoretical framework and an application are provided to clearly explain the foundations and outcomes of this computer tool.

Title: Pie chart or orthogonal diagram? Different levels of effectiveness for graphical images in information transmission.
Author: Aline Jelinski
Abstract: Why are pie charts used more often than orthogonal diagrams? Pie charts are more useful, even indispensable, when the data represents a single entity or whole. Orthogonal diagrams, on the other hand, have the advantage of allowing for precise estimation and ordering of the elements involved.

Title: UML modeling and tools for spatial analysis
Author: Paul-Annick Davoine
Abstract: The implementation of Geographic Information Systems (in the broadest sense of the term) within a spatial analysis framework requires specifying the objectives to be achieved and modeling the domain of study. This therefore implies developing a representation of the reality being studied by describing, on the one hand, the selected geographic objects, their characteristics, and their relationships, and, on the other hand, the processing steps to be performed to meet the established objectives. Recognized as a standard for information system design, the UML (Unified Modeling Language) approach offers numerous models for identifying the static and dynamic structures of computer systems. This approach requires the analysis and structuring of the various parameters and information necessary for implementing these tools. The purpose of this article is therefore to present the specific features of the UML approach, which is in fact an object-oriented modeling language, and to examine its relevance in the design and implementation of spatial analysis tools.

Title: D… as in distogram!
Author: Didier Josselin
Abstract: The Distogram is a tool dedicated to the analysis of statistical and spatial discontinuities, thanks to the dynamic link between a cartographic representation and histograms of descriptive variables. It allows for interactive modification of the number or boundaries of classes, discretization, transformation, and cross-tabulation of variables.

Title: Transportation networks and the optimal location of human activities: a numerical geography approach
Author: Isabelle Thomas
Abstract: This article aims to demonstrate the importance of the shape of the transport network in the optimal location of human activities. Several series of simulations are generated on theoretical networks with square and hexagonal shapes. Common location-allocation models are applied (UFLP, k-median) under different conditions. The results obtained are tested on real networks and concrete land-use planning problems (location of health centers in a region where rainfall affects road accessibility; establishment of waste disposal sites at the municipal level). Several lessons can be drawn from these simulations and examples, particularly in terms of spatial management and land-use planning.

Title: Graphs and fractals. The fractal as a constrained realization and a method for extending and reducing graphs.
Author: Philippe Mathis
Abstract: Recent theses have demonstrated that graphs are well-suited to the functional description of networks, while fractals prove more effective at the morphological level. Graph Theory does not sufficiently specify the conditions and constraints of graph representations. Addressing this deficiency, it can be shown that fractals are specific realizations, as well as a method for extending or reducing graphs that respects the property of internal homothety. We recall that graph realizations, according to Berge, are not based on any assumptions, and that other realizations have been made: a plane or plane projection of a three-dimensional realization by Cauchy, and a sphere and a torus by Lhuillier and Heawood. However, we found partial confirmation of our intuition in Mandelbrot himself. Indeed, its representation of a fractal generator corresponds to that of a graph whose vertices are unnamed, and more specifically to the planar realization of a graph. We demonstrate that the von Koch curve can be described as a graph, and that the internal homothety of the representation also translates into an internal homothety of the adjacency matrix. It then suffices to specify the constraints of the realization to recover the classic geometric fractal. Graphs can also describe fractal trees, as the self-similarity property of the adjacency matrix and the realization is preserved. The Mandelbrot H-fractal can also be represented as a regular tree: these are two realizations of the same graph but under different constraints. Furthermore, this fractal is not necessarily planar. We briefly discuss the example of the Pythagorean tree and the use of primal and quasi-dual concepts. The third example will be the Sierpinski carpet and its application to Christaller theory. This aspect will be extended to Brian Berry's hierarchical rhomboidal systems. Fractals have their correspondences in terms of graph extension and reduction, as do stochastic internal homothety fractals. Finally, we consider the mesh as a limiting case of the fractal, with examples of the square or rectangular H-fractal, triangular and ternary fractal meshes, the hexagonal dual, and then the quasi-dual of an expanding graph. Extended Graph Theory thus has an extension method from the adjacency matrix or realization and symmetrically a reduction method as well as effective morphology indices, which allows considerable progress in the representation and modeling of networks.

Title: The drama of real-life in a time-geographic disguise
Author: Bo Lenntorp
Abstract: A description of a household's daily life, based on time geography, forms the backdrop of this article. The advantages of using time geography notation will be outlined, along with an introduction to some fundamental concepts. The body of the article consists of a discussion of theoretical considerations concerning the foundations of time geography. Particular attention will be paid to the study of certain key concepts, such as contextuality, embodiment, and collateral processes. The interface between the theoretical approach and the graphic notation system will be examined. Significant additional concepts will be highlighted to illustrate the points and provide a basis for potential applications. Some reflections on time geography will be raised to emphasize the pros and cons. Finally, several areas of application will be presented. The conclusion will suggest that time-geography can take on its full value within the framework of both the current debate on the physical and human sciences, and research aimed at considering time and space simultaneously.

Title: Highways, activities and territories: methodological proposals for assessing the impact of highways on the spatial distribution of activities
Author: Emmanuel Faivre
Abstract: Can the highway determine economic activity? This relatively simple, long-standing, and controversial question, posed by the Paris-Rhin-Rhône Motorway Company, remains unresolved despite the acceptance of a logic of interactions taking precedence over a logic of automatic effects from a single element. It essentially encounters a methodological obstacle that, in the current state of research, prevents a more rigorous answer and the dissemination of conclusions validated in all cases. Therefore, we propose a new research method that integrates the entire system of economic activity location and a new research approach that no longer attempts to isolate the highway factor but tries to analyze the role played by the highway within the system to which it belongs. The culmination of our research is the development of a decidedly systemic analytical framework aimed at understanding and explaining the interactions between highways and the system of economic activity location. One of its potential developments lies in its formalization as an expert system.

Title: Game theory and spatial planning: The case of the implementation of the "Grand Besançon" web portal
Author: Oumar Ndiaye
Abstract: Land-use planning is now one of the cornerstones of local government development. Game theory, a branch of economic theory, allows us to analyze the relevance of decisions made by elected officials when considering the management of scarce resources within their territories. From this perspective, game theory can be defined as a theory of decision-making by interdependent economic agents. In this regard, we distinguish between non-cooperative game theory and cooperative game theory. This article seeks to confirm the existence of a method enabling municipalities to pool their resources to optimize their use: waste, energy, water, new information and communication technologies (ICTs), etc. After briefly demonstrating the usefulness of non-cooperative games in the strategic behavior of certain actors, we will focus on cooperative game theory, as it is more relevant to land-use planning. The method we use to conduct our investigations is the Shapley Value Theory. The latter represents the average marginal contribution of each municipality or community, i.e. the value that this community brings in when it joins a coalition.

Title: A complex and multi-territorial production system: The case of microtechnology
Author: Sophie Bergeon-Carel
Abstract: The watchmaking crisis of the 1970s and 1980s led institutions, businesses, and stakeholders in the Franche-Comté region to promote a shift towards microtechnology. However, this attempt to establish a new local production system based on companies originating from the watchmaking industry has been largely unsuccessful. Here, we present the initial findings of research based on the hypothesis of a production system that is no longer local, but rather multi-territorial, organized as a network. It appears to be developing primarily in areas that can be identified in the Paris and Grenoble regions of France, and in Switzerland internationally. The place and role of local watchmaking industries within this configuration remain to be defined. The difficulty in defining the concept of microtechnology itself, coupled with the sector's lack of specificity in industrial statistics, leads us to propose an inductive analysis of the system. This involves observing the practices of manufacturers and identifying the connections between them. From this point of view, the analysis of the Micronora trade fair in Besançon reveals the complexity of the system and helps to guide our future research.

Title: The coastal sea: a pioneering fringe. Essay on the construction of a territorial entity
Author: Brice Trouillet
Abstract: Coastlines are often presented as a major discontinuity, as they materialize one of the boundaries of the inhabited world. If we accept this general principle of a front, it seems that this front is now tending to be complemented by a fringe: the coastal sea. On a global scale, maritime spaces have recently undergone processes of territorialization (in the legal sense). The gradual removal of technical obstacles to the physical occupation of marine and submarine spaces, the discovery of new resources, and the corresponding rise of oceanographic research have made possible the development of modes of spatial occupation previously unknown at sea. The occupation of the coastal sea is becoming increasingly permanent, and the material traces are becoming commonplace: we are witnessing its gradual socialization. Nevertheless, the study of the spatial configuration of the coastal sea reveals, at all scales, a complex and differentiated territorial structure. As a privileged space and time, the territorial systemogenesis in the coastal sea should allow us to reflect on a multifaceted crisis (fisheries, energy, space, etc.) which would condition the speed of pioneering progress and explain the disparities of the pioneering phenomenon.

Title: Evolution of a cross-border production space: one system or several?
Author: Alexandre Moine
Abstract: The spatial organization of a territory owes much to history, to the many actors whose destinies have intersected there, and who, through their decisions, have radically shaped its evolution. In the context of a cross-border territory, the situation becomes even more complex, since the differences created by the state border have weighed, and continue to weigh, on its future. What remains today is a structure, but also, and above all, dynamics marked by past choices and turning points. We therefore address the question of how to represent these facts and the resulting territorial organization. We will trace the history of this territory and represent the systemogenesis of its current spatial structure.

Title: Spatial reproduction, a geohistorical concept for approaching the Roman laboratory
Author: Géraldine Djament
Abstract: This article examines spatial change through a long-term geohistorical analysis of the so-called Eternal City. It begins by defining the concept of reproduction as a dialectic of sameness and otherness in various disciplines, before proposing its application to geography. Applying the concept of spatial reproduction, akin to resilience, to the Roman spatial system involves identifying shifts in urban centrality and studying territorial transitions, particularly the transformation of the religious world-city into the capital of the Italian nation-state. This presentation reveals a veritable "Roman spatial strategy," and outlines the lessons learned from the Roman experience: continuity and discontinuity form a relative and inseparable pair, useful for dividing time and space. The discussion concludes with a plea for geohistory.

Title: Spatial characteristics and automobile pollution in mountainous areas. Diffusion model integrating topography and dispersion capacity applied to the Pyrenean valleys of Biriatou and Aspe (Somport).
Author: Gaëlle Deletraz
Abstract: The aim of this work is to assess the impact of nitrogen pollution from transport on mountain ecosystems. Two Pyrenean valleys were chosen as study sites: the Biriatou site (A63), which is relatively flat, and the Aspe Valley (RN134), which is very narrow and steep-sided, to establish a baseline before the opening of the Somport Tunnel. The pollutant selected for this study is nitrogen dioxide (NO2) because it contributes – along with other nitrogen pollutants – to the acidification and eutrophication of water and soil. The study focuses on two aspects: the dispersion capacity of the different sites and the quantification/spatial mapping of the pollution and associated risks.

Title: The forest facing storm risk: towards further contributions from spatial analysis
Author: Joël Boulier, Claude Grasland
Abstract: Following the storms of December 1999, numerous studies were launched to better understand the impact and behavior of storms in forest environments. The answers provided often focus on the affected stand itself, whether at the individual tree level or at the stand level. However, little attention has been paid to the spatial environment of the affected areas. In this context, we propose a different approach to understanding storm behavior by introducing a strong spatial dimension to the analysis of storm risk and the sensitivity of forest stands. Spatial interaction methods appear to be promising avenues for resolving the problem. Two main lines of inquiry are explored: 1) by considering the direction of airflow, we seek to highlight the interaction between land use and affected areas, according to criteria of distance and the nature of the spatial interaction (potential approach, etc.); 2) Furthermore, we are also focusing our work on the interactions between damage and openings of structures (gaps and enclaves) such as paths, crossroads, roads, clearings… This ambitious program, in addition to its methodological proposals, also seeks to respond to a real expectation of forest stakeholders: can we protect ourselves against the risk of “storms”?

Title: Use of radial analyses to quantify the local landscape scale. Application to the study of the spatio-temporal dynamics of the European water vole
Author: Karine Berthier, Jean-Christophe Foltête, Brigitte Prieur, Jean-François Cosson
Abstract: In landscape ecology, spatial scale is a key element for understanding the influence of spatial variability in the environment on ecological processes. To identify and assess these interactions, ecologists have adapted a wide variety of spatial analyses from other disciplines. In this study, we applied neighborhood analysis, used in soil science, to study a landscape according to spatial scale. This method allows us to identify the local scale of spatial patterns and their degree of heterogeneity through the analysis of radial curves.

Title: Seismic and technological risks. Application to the Mulhouse urban area
Author: Elise Beck, Michel Granet, Christiane Weber
Abstract: The study of interactions between seismic and technological risks in urban areas pursues two objectives: the first is to gain a better understanding of seismic and technological risks in the region studied, and especially of the relationships between them. The second objective is to imagine catastrophic scenarios in order to assess the consequences of a disaster with a view to improving risk management. The Mulhouse metropolitan area (Haut-Rhin, France) is particularly well-suited to such a study because it is an industrial city exposed to technological and natural risks of various kinds (seismic risk, flooding, explosions, fires, pollution).

Title: Evaluating the quality of an intercity transport service: The example of the regional rail network
Author: Hervé Baptiste
Abstract: The law of February 13, 1997, concerning the regionalization of rail transport, followed by the SRU law of 2000, as well as the LOADDT of 1999, have shifted the perception of transport infrastructure towards a more comprehensive intermodal approach that more fully considers the user's perspective. The quality of service offered by the transport network and an understanding of a user's complete journey have become two important entry points for assessing accessibility. By defining the advantages and limitations of several indicators, the aim is to critically examine "traditional" measures and then propose more original ones, based not only on a door-to-door and multimodal approach, but also incorporating timetables for public transport. Starting from "best time" or "frequency" type measures on examples at the national level, we introduce the notion of daily round trip, according to progressive levels of constraints, in order to be able to assess, at the regional level, the possible suitability of transport schedules with the user's lifestyle, or at least their presumed needs.

Title: Urban morphology and pedestrian mobility. Identification of spatial configurations determining the local characteristics of pedestrian movement.
Author: Mehdi Flitti, Arnaud Piombini
Abstract: Pedestrian practices within urban areas remain poorly understood. To better understand this type of movement and thus contribute to its development, this article proposes to study the links between urban morphology and pedestrian mobility. This exploration is based on observing the spatial variations in average walking behaviors dictated by the configuration of the road network in each location. The level of analysis considered is that of the different road segments, where the attributes of pedestrian journeys are aggregated on the one hand, and indicators of urban morphology (network configuration, etc.) on the other. This correlation should allow us to identify spatial configurations that are more or less conducive to pedestrian traffic.

Title: Density, cumulative population, and access time: Analysis of the relationship between urban morphology and access time in the Dijon urban area.
Author: Cyril Enault
Abstract: Conceived as early as 1951, Clark's model is now a benchmark in urban economics for modeling density. However, in 1972, René Bussière developed a new density model much better suited to population data and more capable of describing urban sprawl. Building on this model, Eric Tabourin and Alain Bonnafous, in 1994, proposed a new formalization adapted to both the city and the peri-urban area. This paper aims to test these standard models of urban economics, beginning by verifying the validity of Alonso's monocentric assumptions for Dijon. It is thus shown that the Clark or Bussière models cannot be applied uniformly across the space and that it is necessary to define sectors where the models are feasible. It is then considered that travel time is a much better descriptor than distance to the city center. A method for calculating speeds is developed to determine travel times to the city center. Based on these results, a model aims to demonstrate the non-linearity of time with respect to distance, which, in the event of replacing distance with time, contributes to a reformulation of the Clark and Bussière models. We can then spatialize the Bussière model according to access times, thus highlighting a new temporal break originating with Zahavi and his famous constancy of time budgets.

Title: A multi-scale system for analyzing agrarian dynamics in the savannah zone of the far north of Cameroon
Author: Eric Fotsing, Jean-Paul Cheylan, Wouter T. DeGroot, Peter H. Verburg
Abstract: Agronomic and socio-economic studies at the farm level offer a distinct advantage for understanding the dynamics of agricultural systems. This is the most appropriate scale for identifying the structural elements of the agricultural system and analyzing its organizational logic and management practices. However, studies at the local level already reveal the limitations of these approaches, which are mostly sectoral and disciplinary in nature. Increasingly, experience shows that it is only at the small regional level, and even more so at the regional level, that certain key processes and more pronounced contrasts emerge in land-use systems and their productivity levels. Indeed, identifying appropriate levels of data analysis and representation, as well as developing multi-scale approaches, are becoming increasingly crucial in studies of natural and social systems. This article presents a multi-scale framework designed to analyze the spatial dynamics of the agrarian system in order to develop a model for projecting changes in land use. The spatial hierarchy of the framework is presented, and issues related to scaling methods are then addressed.

Title: Learning German in eastern France: an approach at different geographical levels
Author: Cécile Buxeda
Abstract: This article presents the main theoretical and methodological questions encountered during our doctoral research. Through the study of German language learning, we examine the territorial consequences of the evolving functional nature of the Franco-German border on the greater eastern region of France. The forms of spatial expansion of this practice, studied at different scales, show that it is linked to the proximity of the political border but also reflects a certain persistence of the linguistic boundary. Analyzing language choice behaviors will also allow us to determine whether they are linked to other cross-border practices. To answer these questions, we will attempt to demonstrate the value of an analytical approach conducted at multiple levels of observation.

Title: Mountain landscape and remote sensing. Integration of geomatics tools and digital data into the study of summer pasture landscapes (application to the Pyrenees)
Author: Muriel Harguindéguy
Abstract: In the Pyrenees, summer pastures are high-altitude grazing lands. Sensitive areas, undergoing rapid change, coveted and crucial to a fragile economy, they are receiving particular attention. In this context, a comprehensive understanding of these environments is more necessary than ever to carry out relevant assessments. These assessments require mapping of the environments over large areas. The acquisition of this information can be facilitated by the use of remote sensing, which allows for the production of thematic land-use maps from an applied perspective (maps of pastoral values, potential livestock density, etc.). Our objective is to propose a methodological approach to using radiometric (SPOT XS-P) and topographic (DEM and derived data) information to map – in terms of probabilities – landscape classes and their defining characteristics. It is based on the creation of a typology derived from a Correspondence Analysis (CA) and a Hierarchical Ascending Classification (HAC) performed using detailed field observations (an approach comparable to that of phytosociologists). This is a completely different approach from that of "classic" supervised classifications. To simplify, radiometric and topographic information is used to spatialize (in the sense of providing continuous coverage of) point-based observations whose resolution is lower than that of pixels.

Title: Anamorphoses through pseudo-equivalent transformations. Application to thematic mapping
Author: Patrice Langlois
Abstract: We present a cartographic transformation that allows us to enlarge or shrink map areas based on the values of an associated descriptive variable. We aim for this transformation to have clearly defined spatial properties while producing visually acceptable results. To this end, we have defined a class of elementary polar functions that preserve areas except in the vicinity of the deformation pole; this is the pseudo-equivalence property. We then define a combination operation for these elementary transformations, "progressive composition," which is commutative (i.e., independent of the order in which the elementary transformations are applied) and preserves the pseudo-equivalence property. Finally, we present several thematic maps deformed so that the area sizes become proportional to the associated descriptive values. We analyze the advantages and disadvantages of the different function choices considered.

Title: Towards highlighting a spatial differentiation of household waste collection sectors. Application to the city of Grenoble
Author: Nicolas Perrin
Abstract: Waste management is a growing concern for local authorities, citizens, and businesses. Given the complexity of this issue (multiple schemes and models for household waste management depending on the area, a multitude of stakeholders, and varying scales of action), a more comprehensive approach is necessary. This article will address a recurring information need for waste collection managers: a detailed analysis of household waste collection sectors. Managers seek to streamline and optimize production factors to control waste collection costs. To do this, they need to understand the actual performance of teams in relation to the routes they follow, hence the importance of defining common, accurate, and precise parameters to characterize these routes. However, collection sectors differ from one another and each has its own specific constraints (varying population sizes, distinct percentages of single-family and multi-family housing, number of businesses served, etc.). The aim is to use "fine and rigorous" indicators as well as various socio-economic data to best characterize household waste collection sectors in a GIS.

Title: Methodology for the sustainable management of headwaters. From comprehensive watershed analysis to ecological diagnosis of stream systems.
Author: Raphaël Berthold
Abstract: The new approach to aquatic environment management, embodied in the Water Act of January 3, 1992, and the Water Management and Development Master Plans, necessitates the implementation of methods for more effectively assessing the integrity of these environments. The Ministry of the Environment and the Water Agencies have reconsidered the quality assessment frameworks used in recent decades. The aim is now to evaluate the state of watercourses based on three components: chemical and organic pollutants (Water Quality Assessment System - SEQ-Eau), physical disturbances that destabilize the structure and functioning of watercourses (Physical Quality Assessment System - SEQ-Physique), and finally, biological quality (Biological Quality Assessment System - SEQ-Bio) through bioindicators. However, apart from the Water Quality Assessment System (SEQ-Eau), most of these assessment systems are not operational and are primarily suited to rivers. The objective of this article is to propose a method for assessing the ecological integrity of streams. Its objective is to highlight the influence of human and natural factors on the development of a species of high heritage value: the native brown trout. The value of this approach lies in proposing an assessment system that integrates both biological (Fish Index) and physical (habitat) components in order to evaluate the functional status of these small organisms.

Title: M'Géofoot: software to illustrate the relationship between sport and territory
Author: Frédéric Grosjean, Alexandre Moine
Abstract: Today, the stakeholders in sports are numerous, their development strategies closely intertwined, and the informational resources available for analysis are completely scattered. The challenge of harmonizing the diverse data that describe sports has become crucial. Here, we present the approach to establishing a football observatory (MGéO'FOOT) designed to better manage, organize, and understand the evolution of football within a regional framework. This observatory is being implemented in the Franche-Comté region.

Title: A multi-criteria methodological approach for analyzing a specific event within a long-term timeframe. Application to the evolution of infrastructure and equipment for the Winter Olympic Games in the Alps.
Author: Jocelin Sébastiani
Abstract: To secure the Olympic Games, cities and nations periodically compete in projects that extend far beyond the sporting arena itself: architectural designs for facilities, site development and redevelopment projects, urban development projects, and more. The various facilities built for the Games act as significant drivers of local urban development, transforming the landscape and changing how people use and perceive their living space. We will examine the methods and indicators that can be used to analyze the Olympic phenomenon across five countries in the Alpine region. These are all issues of interest to geographers, given the significant impact the Olympic Games have on a region and a city, leaving a lasting mark on the landscape.

Title: Contribution of Aladin data to the tropospheric ozone forecast in Burgundy
Author: Marie-Laure Houze, Pascale Chevrand, Yves Richard
Abstract: The Regional Climate Change Centre (CRC) and the air quality monitoring networks ATMOSF'air Bourgogne Centre-Nord and Sud are developing a forecasting tool for the aftermath of tropospheric ozone pollution. The objective is to predict daily peak concentrations using statistical models that can be used by the networks.
