These models consider ozone precursors, measured on the day the forecast is made, and the meteorological conditions of that day. The first step was to study the predictability of ozone based on meteorological observations, or "perfect weather forecasts." The second step was to produce actual forecasts. These incorporate meteorological forecasts, which are inherently imperfect: data from the ALADIN numerical model (Limited Area, Dynamic Adaptation, International Development) from Météo-France, with 27- and 36-hour lead times. Forecast performance is higher than predictability performance: the meteorological forecasts from the numerical model are therefore more informative, from an operational point of view, than in-situ measurements. Indeed, modeling compensates for certain shortcomings of observation: in Burgundy, the absence of radiosonde soundings makes it impossible to know the vertical stratification of the atmosphere, a very important parameter with regard to tropospheric ozone concentrations.

Title: The use of climate datasets on general atmospheric circulation models. Concepts, methods and application to the climatology of the South African region
Author: Nicolas Fauchereau, Yves Richard
Abstract: Long-term simulation series using General Atmospheric Circulation (GAC) models—performed by the atmospheric physics community—provide climate geographers with valuable information on climate variability, complementing the analysis of observed series. The study presented here is based on a set of eight long-term simulations (from 1948 to 1997) performed on the French GAC model ARPEGE Climat - Version 3 (National Center for Meteorological Research). These simulations use solar energy and Sea Surface Temperature fields as boundary conditions. Sea Surface Temperatures vary according to monthly observations and are therefore the primary source of interannual variability in atmospheric forcing. The main concepts (forced atmospheric variability versus internal or "chaotic" variability, and atmospheric predictability) are first explained. The statistical methods used (Analysis of Variance and Extended Principal Component Analysis) are then briefly presented. The example given relates to the study of the variability and predictability of rainfall in Southern Africa.

Title: Towards a dynamic model of residential mobility: development in Bogota
Author: Marie Piron, Françoise Dureau, Christian Mullon
Abstract: Within the framework of a research program on spatial mobility and territorial transformations in Bogotá, the capital of Colombia, we aim to dynamically model intra-urban residential mobility and changes in the housing stock. We propose to develop, using game theory, an economic model based on the housing market and, more specifically, on a spatial equilibrium between the advantages and costs of relocating: households seek housing based on the attractiveness of different urban sectors (location, housing stock composition). We combine this model with a demographic model that takes into account the evolution and changes in population and housing stock. To this end, we consider homogeneous groups of households and dwellings. These groups are obtained from typological analyses performed on census data and are geographically defined. We therefore adopt an approach intermediate between the spatial and individual approaches classically used in the development of dynamic urban models.

Title: Landscape representations: what perspectives for planning?
Author: Catherine Caille-Catin
Abstract: Landscape is produced by a community of people who do not necessarily share the same vision for it. Therefore, the perceptions of the various stakeholders—planners, decision-makers, or users—influence how landscape is considered in land-use planning projects. The multiplicity of these perceptions hinders the dialogue that should take place between them when they develop these projects together; however, building consensus is essential. This article will first present an overview of the difficulties that may be encountered, and then, secondly, the methodological approaches used to study landscape perceptions and how they are constructed, in order to understand the factors that influence the choices and practices of these stakeholders regarding landscape management. The analyses will subsequently lead to strategies for improving the integration of landscape considerations into land-use planning operations by these different stakeholders.

Title: Tourist areas represented: a proposed analysis
Author: Céline Tritz
Abstract: The development of the leisure society undoubtedly explains the interest geographers have shown in tourist spaces. Spaces as both produced and consumed, their functional approach has already been well studied. Our predecessors have already developed numerous partial models, for example, to understand the spatial organization of a seaside resort and the diffusion of tourism on a small scale. Alongside this well-studied functional geography, we propose to incorporate a geography of the tourist image. This image-space, approached from the perspective of media coverage, is central to our work. We have chosen a medium for analysis—the tourist guide—and a specific area of study—the Mediterranean arc. We prioritize a spatial approach to media coverage, focusing on its spatial structures. Based on the literal content of the guides, several databases have been created. From this data and by creating images from their spatialization, the use of various spatial analysis methods makes it possible to reveal the spatial structures of places as described by the authors of tourist guides.

Title: Museums of the Great War and territorial identity in Picardy: the petrified territories
Author: Anne Hertzog
Abstract: This article contributes to the geographical analysis of sites of memory, a concept now established in the social sciences but little explored by geographers. It offers an analysis of the spatial dimension of the commemoration of the First World War in Picardy, a region traversed by the front from 1914 to 1918 and the scene of fierce fighting. The approach is comparative: the networks of sites of memory vary in scope and form in each department. This is explained by the different strategies of the actors involved in their structuring: local, national, and also foreign actors, as Picardy is now an international site of memory. A comparison of three foreign museums built in the Somme department will allow for an analysis of the establishment of transnational networks whose organization is reminiscent of diasporic phenomena. Finally, the role of landscape in the transmission of memory will be examined.

Title: Travel and landscape: a meeting of images
Author: Lucie Fontaine
Abstract: By its very nature, a journey unfolds within a landscape, but the relationship between landscape and travel is more complex than simply traversing a space. Before setting off, we dream of our trip; once there, we encounter a space; and upon returning, only memories remain. According to J.-D. Urbain, the desire to travel is defined by three models of representation into which the traveler projects themselves; the one that particularly interests us here is that of the “space of travel” or “model of the world,” of which the landscape, the visible form of the territory, then becomes the “sign.” By measuring the gap between representations, perceptions, and the reality of a landscape, we can identify the landscape motifs that guide the choice of a journey and thus try to grasp their importance within these “models of the world.”

Title: Virtual landscapes and territorial projects
Author: Sandrine Alinat
Abstract: Landscape modeling appears as an attractive method for facilitating the involvement of local stakeholders. Realistic, aesthetically pleasing landscape representations are a key factor in decision-making for development projects. However, they are sometimes poorly suited to validating territorial scenarios. The example of a forest expansion project will allow us to examine the relevance and applicability of these new IT tools used to support negotiation and decision-making in territorial development projects.

Title: Functionality and vulnerability of transport networks. The case of the Paris metro
Author: Jean-François Gleyze
Abstract: Natural and man-made disasters threaten to damage transport networks, not only structurally but also functionally by causing disruptions through diversions. In this context, we chose to study the operation of the Paris metro network in both normal and damaged modes. First, we define and quantify the network's efficiency for its assigned role. We then characterize the functional role of the network's various components in normal operating mode. Based on this study, we finally consider the possibility of disasters and examine the network's potential in terms of alternative routes, firstly using a synthetic index derived from transport research, and secondly, within the context of specific damage scenarios. The conclusions of this work shed light on the network's operation from a risk prevention perspective.

Title: Scalar and temporal dynamics of port cities. A global typology of 330 urban-port trajectories, 1990-2000
Author: César Ducruet
Abstract: Based on an analysis of extensive literature, this research aims to highlight the complex transformations occurring in port cities worldwide. In a context of ongoing restructuring of containerized maritime transport and continental shipping routes, the increased mobility of flows appears to be increasingly at odds with urban dynamics at multiple simultaneous geographical levels. The creation of a global database covering more than three hundred hubs allows us to analyze the changes that have occurred in the recent period (1990-2000). The spatio-functional model of growing incompatibility between urban and port functions is thus qualified by the results of a factor analysis of temporal variations, leading to a strong regional differentiation in port city trajectories.

Title: Locoregional analysis model of energy systems
Author: Khaled Ibrahim, Marie-Hélène De Sède-Marceau
Abstract: The major challenge facing all actors in the energy system today is to account for the simultaneously contradictory relationships between globalization and decentralization, on the one hand, and between socio-economic development and sustainable development, on the other. This challenge must be addressed through a comprehensive approach, the only one capable of grasping the full complexity of the problem, induced by the interactions of socio-economic, political, technological, and environmental factors. This approach must be conducted by situating the energy system within a territorial framework that allows for understanding the logic and spatial implications of the system's various components. In this sense, a systemic model of a territorial energy system is proposed. This results in two levels of representation and analysis: first, an organizational and evolutionary diagram representing the energy system as a set of interacting elements (content) within a spatio-temporal framework (container); Next, an energy system analysis grid is developed, combining two approaches: a local/regional territorial approach (from the local to the regional level) and dynamic analysis. Based on this grid, a methodological framework is proposed for developing a dynamic information and simulation system for territorial energy systems at the local/regional scale, the outlines of which we have defined in terms of architecture and formalization methods.

Title: How to assess and represent the change in Bogotá's social structure? Levels of observation in the analysis of change
Author: Marie Piron
Abstract: The aim of this study is to analyze the structural changes in the social composition of Bogotá between 1973 and 1993 and to examine how these changes are spatially organized. To this end, we propose using multidimensional exploratory analysis tools and conduct a comparative analysis of partition hierarchies at different dates. This offers several advantages. First, because these tools are robust and well-suited to highlighting the city's social forms, even a minor change in structures between two dates appears significant and meaningful. Second, it allows us to progressively observe the changes in Bogotá's social composition; comparing the typologies for the two years, using different levels of granularity, reveals how social forms are modified, persist, disappear, or emerge over the study period. The method is qualitative and demonstrates how the analysis of changes in social structure depends on the level of observation.

Title: Measuring urban "cultural potential"
Author: Françoise Lucchini
Abstract: This research sheds light on the collective cultural forms perceptible in contemporary society: a "culture in the plural," opening up possible practices for individuals. The constructivist approach employed leads to an evaluation of the cultural offerings available to city dwellers. These offerings comprise various cultural and artistic services and facilities present in cities, as well as specialized education, both academic and more accessible. The geographical configurations of this cultural system, the divergent or similar political strategies, and the cultural hubs are thus observed in France, the United Kingdom, and Quebec—that is, in different national political contexts—to test the robustness of the "global cultural system" that emerges. A multi-scalar investigation is proposed. Ultimately, a simple and transferable measure of the cultural offerings within urban neighborhoods is presented. This cultural potential is calculated based on an urban grid. The resulting map of "cultural potential" reveals the existence of different cultural poles, or "centers of gravity" of this spatial phenomenon, i.e. of the distribution of cultural offerings in the city in quantity and variety.

Title: Analysis and assessment of flood vulnerability in the lower Orge basin
Author: Bruno Barroca, Nathalie Pottier, Emilie Lefort
Abstract: This article presents the development of a vulnerability assessment tool for flooding a tributary of the Seine upstream of Paris and its application to the urbanized part of the catchment area. The reflections presented stem from an exploratory approach based on extensive literature review preceding field studies and interviews with key local stakeholders. The assessment tool developed allows for the analysis and evaluation of local vulnerability to urban flooding according to several factors: hazard vulnerability (1), population vulnerability (2), building vulnerability (3), land use vulnerability (4), and crisis management vulnerability (5). Each of these five factors is analyzed and assessed using a grid that allows for the development of vulnerability indicators based on detailed lists of criteria. These grids, developed in consultation with practitioners and risk managers, constitute a decision-making tool within the framework of integrated management of urban areas subject to flooding. The emphasis is placed on the methodological aspect of the tool and not on the results specific to the site studied (the lower Orge site).

Title: Automatic detection and mapping of rural villages in developing countries using remote sensing and spatial analysis
Author: Nicolas Devaux
Abstract: Large-scale mapping data relating to population distribution, such as the individual location of dwellings, is essential for many land-use planning projects. However, its availability is virtually nonexistent in rural areas of developing countries, where existing mapping data is over fifty years old and rarely exceeds a scale of 1:50,000. Decentralized rural electrification (DRE), carried out by ADEME and EDF in developing countries, is an example of a local development project that requires the precise location of dwellings to make informed technical decisions. The advent of high spatial resolution (HRS) and very high spatial resolution (VHSR) satellite data can provide alternatives to the current situation by producing up-to-date mapping data at scales that meet specific needs. However, the automation of data processing necessitates the adoption of new methods to overcome the limitations of purely radiometric approaches. The spatial approach, by emphasizing the consideration of the spatial organization of the areas studied through automated classification processes, yields promising results. This article proposes a development of the methodological approach and its application to the delimitation of villages in the Far North region of Cameroon.

Title: The solid angle, a tool for reading the landscape
Author: Jean Duchesne, Vincent Bouvier, Céline Dreyer
Abstract: The research presented here focuses on studying the relationship between the quantification of geometric parameters through the measurement of solid angles (easily linked to the concepts of visual screen and gap) and the interpretation of the landscape. This approach considers the three dimensions of space. The concept of solid angle can be proposed as a tool for analyzing landscape forms. The solid angle corresponds to the measurement of the projection of an object's shape onto a sphere from a given observation point. The article first clarifies the context in which such a tool can be used and explains the concept of solid angle. Second, it presents the calculation methods in relation to some principles of spherical trigonometry, using two measurement methods: one with an in-situ theodolite and the other from two-dimensional photographs of the landscape. Third, a discussion considers the relevance and future prospects of such an approach.

Title: Moving through the landscape. An attempt to model visibility from the roads of Franche-Comté.
Author: Sébastien Nageleisen
Abstract: There are multiple meanings of the term and concept of landscape, and consequently, multiple methods for studying it. Geographers typically approach landscape in its entirety, treating each point in space as a potentially visible landscape. This conception distances them from the usual practices of those who use the space. Indeed, these users discover and experience landscape through various routes and modes of travel, which define a succession of images based on the panoramas and viewpoints offered. Given this observation, it is worthwhile to reintroduce, into the geographical approach, the terms of landscape discovery as they result from the everyday practices of users. This formalization, which considers only the potential for visibility rather than the phenomena of perception, can be developed on reasoned and experimental grounds, thanks to the resources offered by computer data. This article represents only a small part of a much larger project that essentially combines two methodologies: GIS visibility analysis and image bank analysis. The article focuses solely on the former, applied to analyzing the visibility potential of roads in the Franche-Comté region.

Title: Oblique terrestrial photography for environmental monitoring in the Arctic environment (webcam of the Zeppelin Fjellet, 79°N, Spitsbergen)
Author: Madeleine Griselin, Sébastien Nageleisen, Serge Ormaux, Kim Holmén, Dominique Laffly
Abstract: Oblique photography taken from the Earth's surface can become a complementary tool to the projection imagery (aerial photography and satellite imagery) typically used in remote sensing. For a relatively low implementation cost, it allows for environmental monitoring at particularly fine spatial and temporal scales, despite the low image resolution. In the Arctic, standard meteorological data poorly capture the dynamics of snow and sea ice. Yet, these are two fundamental components of the polar environment that can be understood from a landscape perspective. Since May 2000, a webcam has been installed on the Zeppelin Fjellet (78°53'N, 11°53'E, 474 m altitude). For over four years, it has provided 24 images per day, offering a panoramic view of King's Bay and the Ny Ålesund station. The 36,000 images in this collection represent a considerable source of information—freely available online—on a region particularly responsive to global change. While the orthorectified images allow for surface area assessments, the raw images offer a wealth of information regarding the foreground features (sandur and fjord). The image bank allows for the identification of snow and sea ice cover types. These types occur over time in sequences exhibiting significant interannual variability, which can be correlated with meteorological data (air temperature, precipitation, wind speed and direction). Ultimately, we plan to use a network of digital cameras connected to intervalometers that will automatically provide extensive data specifically for analyzing particular phenomena. Thanks to a dozen photographic stations installed on a small frozen basin (Loven East), it will be possible to extract quantitative information about the snowpack from the oblique image and thus deduce the water depth corresponding to the melting over the 10 km2 basin.

Title: Interaction patterns in multi-agent systems
Author: Benoît Glisse
Abstract: Interactions play a crucial role in the dynamics of multi-agent systems. Modelers need to create interaction mechanisms that reflect their knowledge and assumptions in order to build their models. However, the available options are virtually endless, especially since similarity between the interactional model and the observed environment is rarely an end in itself. This similarity stems either from a deliberate modeling choice or from the impossibility of obtaining a simulation. The problem of choosing an appropriate representation poses a significant challenge to the use of multi-agent systems. This article aims to highlight the richness of interactional models for multi-agent systems and to situate them within the broader context of the modeling process. From this perspective, the organizational role of interactional models will first be discussed through various general solutions and then detailed with a few examples.

Title: Towards a geography of interspatiality: The Roman example
Author: Géraldine Djament
Abstract: This article proposes a transfer of the literary notion of intertextuality to geography. The example of the pilgrimage to the Seven Churches, borrowed from Counter-Reformation Rome, shows that a reference to another space can structure the practice of a space: the journey around Rome is doubled by an imaginary journey around Christendom and Jerusalem. The notion of interspatiality allows us to theorize such a practice. Just as intertextuality has revealed the dialogic dimension of each text, interspatiality represents a new type of spatial interaction, belonging to the domain of spatial representations. From this perspective, modern Rome is presented as a laboratory of interspatiality. It uses numerous spatial references and also constitutes a space of reference for other cities: it proves to be at the center of a complex interspatial system. Finally, this article calls for a generalization by outlining a classification of interspatialities and by questioning the functions – in particular of legitimation – of such cospatiality.

Title: The territory as a complex system. Tools for planning and geography
Author: Alexandre Moine
Abstract: Territories are now at the forefront, under pressure to provide socio-economic development solutions or a coherent image of the places they encompass. We are witnessing a widespread use of the concept that everything is territory; and concepts covering other realities are imperceptibly shifting towards this now very general notion, which represents everything and nothing at the same time. We therefore wanted to revisit it from a systemic perspective, in order to produce an operational definition that allows us to reposition territory in relation to geographical space. The defined territory is thus placed back at the heart of complexity.

Title: The dilemma of the spatially confined prisoner. Application to territorial cooperation
Author: Michel Bussi, Eric Daudé
Abstract: Territorial cooperation has become a major issue in spatial planning and development policies. Spatial planning is now less of an authoritarian, top-down process and more of an incentive for emerging cooperation among local territories, which are encouraged to work together within relevant boundaries. Examples include the additionality of funding for infrastructure projects between local authorities, the increasing use of territorial contracts, and the development of inter-municipal cooperation with its own tax base. However, the assumption of spontaneous cooperation between territories may seem utopian, since every decision-maker, even if altruistic, will primarily act in the best interests of the territory they represent. Territorial cooperation only appears truly credible within a "win-win" strategy. The question thus posed "why would territories cooperate in a context of competitive economy between territories?" clearly refers to the work of Robert Axelrod (1984) on theories of cooperative behavior, and more generally on the reflections of game theory around the "prisoner's dilemma".

Title: Territorial development and post-Fordism: What are the implications for employment in Switzerland?
Author: Christophe Mager
Abstract: This paper proposes an analytical framework that can help interpret employment trends in Switzerland between 1985 and 2001, based on the post-Fordist hypothesis that the most economically successful regions are now those capable of mobilizing endogenous resources, irreducible to a single productive structure, referred to as "regional effects" (local culture, formal and informal institutions, relational capital, interconnections, etc.) (Amin, 2003; Fontan, 2003). The econometric model of R. Marimoni and F. Zilibotti (1998) will be used to identify in which employment areas and for which industrial and service sector activities these regional effects were most significant. The analyses will allow for: the identification of a set of regions potentially generating regional best practices to be analyzed in more detail (local production systems, governance, etc.); and the identification, for each region analyzed, of the sectors in which these best practices could be effective. We will conclude, based on the results obtained, by questioning, on the one hand, the relevance, in Switzerland, of the post-Fordist hypothesis according to which the current capitalist development model seeks a spatiality of its own reflecting its internal relations and favouring metropolitan spaces and, on the other hand, its innovative character in relation to traditional approaches to spatial economics (Krugman, 1998).

Title: Analysis of the spatial distribution of ozone concentrations in Burgundy. Preliminary results
Author: Marie-Laure Houze, Thierry Castel, Yves Richard
Abstract: A campaign to measure tropospheric ozone using passive scattering tubes was conducted in August 2000 across the entire Burgundy region to better understand the spatial distribution of concentrations at the regional scale. As expected, the results showed different daytime and nighttime ozone concentrations. This day/night variability appears to be associated with a superposition of signals with different spatial and temporal scales. As a first approximation, we considered the ozone concentrations measured in the region as the sum of several signals of different frequencies: a "low-frequency"—or background—signal, which we sought to eliminate in order to focus on the high-frequency signal of local origin—i.e., the residual signal. The spatial correlation of this residual value was then characterized by the calculation and modeling of experimental semi-variograms. The preliminary analysis and interpretation of this structure were finally conducted using a GIS, by combining different layers of information on surface properties and atmospheric states across the entire air column. The results show, for certain dates, the predominance of dispersive effects on the spatial distribution of ozone concentrations. These effects are strongly modulated according to the configurations (atmospheric states and concentration levels) by surface properties (roughness).

Title: Exploring the effect of different types of mobility on the spread of epidemics
Author: Eric Daudé, Emmanuel Eliot
Abstract: Few studies consider the spread of disease through the lens of mobility behaviors, which are fundamental epidemiogenic factors. Indeed, human vectors exhibit different mobility behaviors that can have varying effects on the configuration of epidemics. Here, several types of mobility are tested. These consider not only the forms of circulation (linear, circular) but also its rhythms (with or without stops). To explore the behavior of these hypotheses and their impact on the dynamics of propagation, different agent-based models are implemented and subjected to simulation.

Title: The origins of seaside urbanization on the southern Breton or Vendée coast
Author: Johan Vincent
Abstract: For some authors, the seafront risks becoming nothing more than a line of houses and apartment buildings, due to rampant speculation along the shoreline. However, this debate about urbanization is not new; it even arose following the urbanization of the coastline in 19th-century France. Investing on the coast at that time was a risky undertaking. Reflecting on the motivations for settling on the coast of southern Brittany and the Vendée region helps us understand the mechanisms that created the coastline as we know it today. The arrival of a new population driven by a new trend, the transformation and accessibility of the shoreline that made this territory viable—several steps were necessary before urbanization became possible.

Title: Landscape iconography and knowledge about landscapes: A methodological proposal for evaluating landscape representations disseminated by landscape atlases to stakeholders in land-use planning.
Author: Catherine Caille-Catin
Abstract: Landscape atlases were conceived as early as 1994 as potential tools for landscape knowledge. Their authors inventory and analyze regional landscapes. Decision-making can thus be facilitated by processing the information contained in the atlas. The images (texts, photographs, maps, sketches, etc.), as representations of the landscapes they comprise, reveal and enrich social representations of the landscape through the nature of the information disclosed, thereby promoting certain landscape approaches. The visual images and texts contained in landscape atlases therefore generate mental landscape representations for planning stakeholders that echo their initial representations. These initial representations are developed through their various experiences—individual, professional, etc.—and constitute a repertoire of more or less elaborate concepts upon which stakeholders will interpret and filter the information necessary for the landscape knowledge they need to design planning projects. The choice of iconographic and textual information thus appears paramount for the design of landscape atlases. Observing and analyzing the landscape knowledge tools available to land-use planning stakeholders will allow us to identify the specific features highlighted by various project owners and managers in landscape atlases. This research will reveal diverse communication strategies employed by these stakeholders. Our presentation will outline the methodological protocol for this study and the analyses conducted.

Title: Landscape perception surveys using photographs: Methodological choices and examples in a riverine environment
Author: Yves-François Le Lay, Hervé Piegay, Mélanie Cossin
Abstract: Numerous landscape perception surveys have been conducted using ground-level photographs. A literature review presents the different paradigms within which these surveys have been carried out. Methodological options are then presented to clarify the justification for using photographs and to explain how to construct a photo-questionnaire. The number of photographs and their selection are discussed. The value of different attitude scales (notably the Likert scale and the visual analog scale) is also addressed. Furthermore, the results of three surveys illustrate the relevance of these approaches, highlighting their strengths and limitations. These surveys were conducted on river landscapes, focused on evaluating planning policies, and carried out within the framework of psychophysical and cognitive paradigms. Overall, the aim is to elucidate the contribution of such surveys to the work of managers in terms of decision-making, as they allow for the exploration of modeling and the anticipation of reactions based on the structuring elements of landscapes.

Title: Cognitive representations of urban space among adolescents: A first methodological approach to age-related disparities
Author: Kaira Hamza
Abstract: Cognitive representations of space are internalized mental entities constructed by individuals in relation to their interactions with the environment. The result of numerous mental and dynamic processes, they are not static and differ from one individual to another. This article presents the cognitive representations that adolescents aged 12 to 18 have of the city of Belfort, a test city. More specifically, it addresses the disparities observed in representations of urban space at different ages of adolescence. The article presents the entire methodological approach implemented to study these disparities: from the formulation of the hypothesis, which stipulates that cognitive representations of urban space vary among adolescents according to age, to the analysis of the results.

Title: Proposal for spatial modeling and formalization of on-demand transport (TAD)
Author: Elodie Castex
Abstract: Demand-responsive transport (DRT) is a form of public ground transport "that combines the advantages of public transport and private vehicles" (Banos & Josselin, 1999). Since the late 1990s, the number of DRT services has been steadily increasing. This development has been accompanied by a diversification of operating and organizational structures across a variety of territories, from dense urban areas to isolated rural areas, at both the municipal and departmental levels. Consequently, it has become difficult to establish a representative typology of these services. In order to create a reliable classification of the different DRT systems, this article proposes to examine a little-studied aspect of DRT: its spatial dimension. To this end, we propose a method for describing forms of spatial service based on territorial organization, the origins and destinations of journeys, and service constraints.

Title: The construction of theoretical votes. An application of the Johnston model to the results of the first round of the 2002 presidential elections.
Author: Céline Colange
Abstract: In a context often characterized by the "nationalization" of voting behavior, maps of the geography of votes following the first round of the 2002 presidential election reveal a clear reorganization of vote distribution. A misalignment along traditional regional or sociological lines has given way to a partisan realignment linked to the rural-urban divide. This article emphasizes the strong socio-spatial structuring of votes, particularly votes for new parties, using Johnston's model, which combines ecological and qualitative data. Similarly, through a novel methodology that reconstructs votes based on distance from urban areas, this research demonstrates the impact of the urban gradient as an explanatory factor in voting behavior—a factor that remains predominant even after controlling for the effects of social structure. This analysis also offers some avenues for reflection on understanding the territorialization of the far-right vote, which intensified in peri-urban areas. The peri-urban area now appears as a new spatial component that must be taken into consideration.

Title: Local indicators of spatial association (LISA) as a method of regionalization. An application in India
Author: Sébastien Oliveau
Abstract: In India, census data are of sufficiently high quality to allow for a detailed geographical approach to socio-economic phenomena at the municipal level. However, the significant variability of the data at this scale, as well as the large number of units to consider, makes it difficult to present synthetic results that would highlight the major structures of the studied area. Our objective is to present a solution that, to use Gould's expression, "lets the data speak for themselves." This involves revealing regional trends while preserving the detail of the municipal data. To achieve this, we use local spatial autocorrelation indices that allow us to measure the similarities (and dissimilarities) between neighboring areas. Local spatial association indicators (LISA), developed by Luc Anselin (1995), allow us to measure the degree of resemblance between a spatial unit and its neighbors. This approach allows us to reveal regional trends while preserving local values, that is, to maintain information about the internal heterogeneity of these areas. Our presentation will first introduce LISAs (Local Area Statistics) from a statistical perspective, a necessary step to understand how these indicators function and the inherent limitations of their construction. We will then propose an application where we use these indicators to create an original spatial division of Tamil Nadu. This state, located in southeastern India, currently has over 62 million inhabitants spread across more than 16,000 municipalities, providing a remarkable framework for testing the effectiveness of this method.

Title: Uncertainty in a climate data spatialization process
Author: Rémi Lhotellier
Abstract: In the process of spatializing climate data from point measurements, it is necessary to consider all levels of imprecision and uncertainty inherent in each stage of the modeling, from the measurement itself to the validity of the resulting field. The working context—namely, the type of data used, the scale of the study, and the terrain's topography—must highlight the cumulative uncertainties within this process, as well as allow for their quantification and mapping. Every thematic map must therefore be accompanied by a quality of estimation map. The case presented here concerns the spatialization of air temperature in four predominantly Alpine French departments.

Title: The urban hydrological graph: structuring data to determine the flow of water in the city
Author: Aleksandra Barczak
Abstract: Stormwater runoff is among the urban hazards with a strong anthropogenic component. This paper aims to contribute to the assessment of runoff hazard through an analysis of a basic hydrological process: the path of water from the points where it falls on the surface of the catchment to its outlet. To trace the path of water through the city, a procedure for constructing an urban hydrological graph will be proposed. Through network analysis, we will be able to describe the path of water in three dimensions, taking into account the formation of runoff on urban or natural surfaces, runoff concentrated on slopes and roads, and finally its underground path before reaching the receiving environment. The spatial information thus obtained will then be used to study various hydrological parameters, to analyze the morphology of the networks, and finally, it will serve as a basis for the development of a hydrological model.

Title: Probability of occurrence of a parasitic phenomenon and choice of logistic regression models
Author: Florian Tolle, François Pierre Tourneux
Abstract: Epidemiological processes are increasingly being addressed using spatial statistics and modeling tools. This work generally aims to highlight outbreaks and identify variables that can explain their presence. The binary nature of health data necessitates the implementation of specific methods such as binary logistic regression, which assigns each sample a probability of presence of the pathogen of interest. The subsequent classification of each sample requires choosing a probability threshold to define whether the observations are risky or not. The ROC method allows for the definition of this threshold and a precise understanding of the consequences of this choice. Using a point epidemiological database, several models were generated and tested. Landscape indices were derived in the environment of the points at three scales of analysis. The probabilities assigned to each sample by the models were spatially represented, providing a tool for interpreting the expected distribution of contaminated samples. The variables identified at these three scale levels led to the development of hypotheses regarding the landscape factors involved in epidemiological processes. The emergence of potential risk hotspots constitutes a first finding.

Title: Identification of domino effects following an earthquake. Application to the Mulhouse urban area
Author: Élise Beck, Christiane Weber, Michel Granet
Abstract: Risks in urban environments are a growing concern that warrants moving beyond single-sector studies that consider only one risk at a time. Indeed, given the domino effects observed in recent years, it is necessary to study risks from a comprehensive perspective and identify potential domino effects. In this research, our objective was to identify industrial accidents likely to occur following a major earthquake. Based on determining physical vulnerability to earthquakes and characterizing the function of buildings, this method was applied to the Mulhouse metropolitan area, which is exposed to seven hazards of varying natures. The results indicate that four accidents could occur following an earthquake; the worst-case scenario involves the release of toxic substances within a 130-meter radius of one of the buildings at an industrial site located in western Mulhouse. Thus, the effects would not reach the residential sector adjacent to the industrial site but would slightly exceed the site's footprint to the north.

Title: Urban cultural offerings in Europe: points of comparison
Author: Virginie Cremades
Abstract: This article summarizes the initial findings of a comparative study on urban cultural offerings in Europe. Adopting a broad definition of culture, the study examines these offerings through a non-exhaustive range of permanent (museums, etc.) and periodic (festivals, etc.) cultural facilities, as well as exceptional events (European Capital of Culture, etc.). The study focuses on 244 European urban areas with populations exceeding 200,000, located in the 27 countries of the European Union, Switzerland, and Norway. The aim of this research is to determine whether, in the current context of globalization, we are faced with a homogeneous or differentiated cultural offering in medium-sized and large European urban areas. It also explores the role of urban hierarchy and urban functions in shaping these offerings. Multivariate statistical analyses were performed on the collected data. The initial results show a link between the cultural offering (quantitative) and the urban hierarchy, but it is necessary to qualify this in terms of its diversity (qualitative).

Title: Methods of representing the daily trajectories of inhabitants - Exploration of spatio-temporal data
Author: Elodie Cochey, Kamila Tabaka
Abstract: Recent research on daily mobility has shown that individual mobility strategies are centered around activity schedules. In France, Household Travel Surveys (EMD) are one of the main sources of information on mobility behavior. Although these surveys were not designed to analyze activity schedules, they provide an important source of spatio-temporal data, but one that requires adaptation. This study is based on the Household Travel Survey conducted in the Grenoble region in 2002. We propose to explore the daily mobility of Grenoble residents by selecting a few individual examples to show how space and time are used in organizing activities throughout the day. To this end, three approaches will be used: the spatial approach, the temporal approach, and the spatio-temporal approach. We use a visualization tool called Traj'Net, following a multidimensional exploratory analysis phase that allowed us to distinguish different profiles of daily mobility behavior. The three types of representation proposed are complementary and help to compare individuals' uses of space and time. Furthermore, they raise new questions for future studies of spatiotemporal trajectories.

Title: Study of color contrasts to improve map readability - application to risk maps
Author: Elisabeth Chesneau
Abstract: Maps are designed and used in many fields (geography, history, economics, ecology, etc.). Some of the topics covered are particularly difficult to map, notably because the data is abundant and overlapping, as in risk maps. This often leads to maps that are difficult to read and therefore cumbersome to use. We propose to investigate the parameters that influence map readability, particularly the role of color. To this end, we choose an interdisciplinary approach (cartography, psychology, painting) which leads us to define two types of reference data: a color palette and a theory on their contrasts, that of the Swiss painter Itten. Given this knowledge base, a model for the automatic improvement of color contrasts in maps is created: through iterative cycles, the worst color contrasts in the map are improved. An ARiCo prototype, developed for risk maps, serves to validate our model.

Title: A new approach to proximity for optimal location studies
Author: Marie-Noëlle Comin, Joël Boulier
Abstract: Proximity is a relative concept and varies considerably from one geographical environment to another. Generally, the definition of proximity used in optimal location studies is that of the nearest supply site. Thus, location-allocation models, such as the p-median model, typically allocate the relevant population to the nearest supply site. In this article, we propose a relative approach to the concept of "proximity" in the field of optimal location, which amounts to defining it according to the specific spatial context of each demand point. To do this, we modify the demand allocation rule for supply sites by introducing a notion of a natural threshold specific to each demand point. This natural threshold represents a distinct jump in the order of distances to be traveled from a demand point to a supply site. However, this proximity approach remains a research avenue since it has not yet been rigorously validated, requiring real confrontation with reality, particularly through a meticulous study of users' spatial behavior.

Title: The city as a potential for social interactions
Author: Cyrille Genre-Grandpierre, David Perrussel-Morin
Abstract: In this article, the city is defined as a potential for interaction, as a capacity to connect with others. This level of potential depends not only on population density (which explains why density is often associated with urbanity) but also on mobility capabilities. Therefore, we propose a functional, rather than morphological, exploration of urban and peri-urban spaces through the calculation of the potential for social interaction (PSI). Being in a city then means having a certain level of PSI in a given location, which can lead to an attempt at a functional delimitation of the urban. After defining PSI as the number of individuals with whom it is possible to connect within 20 minutes from a given point using a specific mode of transport, we examine the spatial and historical variations of PSI. These variations are then addressed from an economic perspective, as mobility capabilities are limited by individuals' budgets. Finally, we seek to separate in the observed values of the PIS, the respective contribution of the population distribution and the road network, which leads us to the conclusion that the city is primarily made of speed rather than spatial configurations.

Title: Landscape postcards: a tool for territorial analysis
Author: Jean-Baptiste Litot, Arnaud Piombini
Abstract: The quintessential image of tourism, the landscape postcard, remains a relatively underutilized medium in the humanities and social sciences, and is even entirely absent from geography. Yet, as a privileged vehicle for conveying the image of a place within another, it can shed light on our understanding of the structure of tourist territories, their promotion, and the mechanisms involved in the spatial dissemination of images of tourist sites. Thus, we demonstrate the possibilities offered by this uncommon medium while identifying the factors influencing landscape mediation. To this end, we propose a statistical method for measuring and weighting the influence of the various factors tested. The results obtained reveal the essential role of seemingly obvious factors, such as the distance between tourist sites and points of sale, but other, less predictable factors also have a significant impact, such as the landscape itself.

Title: Identifying "dominant variables" in landscape organization: a multi-scale approach
Author: Pierre-Olivier Mazagol
Abstract: Managing a territory like the Hautes Chaumes du Forez, which possesses a certain uniqueness, requires a thorough understanding of the factors and processes that contribute to its organization. Here, we propose a methodology, centered on the Pegase process, highlighting the physical and anthropogenic variables that play a crucial role. Using the concept of spatial entropy, we demonstrate the importance of scale effects, and their consideration allows for the selection of these variables, which we call dominant.

Title: Delineation of morphological units using a multi-scale approach. Application to the morphological delineation of urban areas.
Author: Cécile Tannier, Gilles Vuidel, Pierre Frankhauser
Abstract: This article focuses on identifying the boundary of built-up areas, which we define as the limit of an area exhibiting a coherent spatial structure across different scales. We approach this question from a purely morphological perspective, within a multi-scale framework. After first establishing the research context, we present the methodological principles underlying the identification of the boundary of built-up areas. The first step of the methodology, namely the step-by-step expansion of the built-up area under study, is briefly described. Emphasis is placed on the second step, which is the identification of a threshold in the curve resulting from the expansions. The third chapter of the article provides an opportunity to present some examples of the application of the methodology to theoretical cases, while the fourth and final chapter focuses on its application to the morphological delimitation of urban areas.

Title: Proposal for a renewed approach to territorial evaluation
Author: Laure Casanova
Abstract: The introduction of sustainable development principles into spatial planning has led to a proliferation of territorial assessment and forecasting initiatives. However, the theoretical and methodological foundations of these approaches are neither consensual nor stable, making the analytical processes often difficult to replicate and the results of limited practical application. This research position proposes an example of a renewed approach to territorial assessment by utilizing spatial analysis tools. A prospective indicator of the state of territories is developed and then tested in the Provence-Alpes-Côte d'Azur region.

Title: Measures of corporate group anchoring: An application to French agricultural cooperative groups
Author: Maryline Filippi, Olivier Frey, Pierre Triboulet
Abstract: The processes of localizing and relocating activities demonstrate the influence of space on corporate strategies. The development of corporate groups and the increasing number of mergers and acquisitions are altering the spatial organization of firms. This paper aims to analyze the spatial embeddedness of corporate groups. Its conceptual framework is based on proximity analysis and theories of the firm. The study focuses on agricultural cooperative groups whose territorial embeddedness is being challenged by the significant growth of subsidiaries. The groups were identified using national databases (LIFI and EAE 2003). Two indicators are proposed to measure the spatial embeddedness of the groups in relation to the activities developed and the different units of analysis (establishment, company, group). The results highlight a strong anchoring around the parent cooperatives. However, this anchoring should be qualified by the possibility of a shift in spatial logic within large cooperative groups that concentrate an increasing share of activity.

Title: Calibration of households preference for open-spaces from an urban cellular automata model - Method and application to Dijon
Author: Geoffrey Caruso, Mohamed Hilal
Abstract: We propose a calibration method for a residential growth model that is grounded on a micro-economic cellular automation. This model can be seen as a spatial and dynamic representation of an urban economic model with neighborhood externalities. A 2D spatial equilibrium of residential locations is obtained stepwise through time instead of being a one-shot instantaneous equilibrium. Previous research work showed that the model can produce more or less dense and fragmented urban patterns depending on the preference of households for open space. We propose here a method for calibrating those preferences from simulations of the model and land rents observed within the Dijon urban area. More precisely, equilibrium properties of the model are used to derive the elasticity of open-space preferences. Then simulations are used to estimate the neighborhood distance to which open-space are valued by households. Our first results tend to support our residential behavior assumptions and tend to be in accordance with results obtained with more classic methods. Further methodological improvements are however needed.

Title: Hierarchical structures in geography: from linear models to non-linear models (power laws and log-periodic corrections)
Author: Maxime Forriez, Philippe Martin
Abstract: The power law (and especially the rank-size law) is used in many empirical models in geography. Often, an oscillation of experimental points can be observed on logarithmic graphs. Until recently, these oscillations were interpreted as artifacts. Thanks to recent mathematical developments, these fluctuations can be modeled by a log-periodic fractal law, as we will demonstrate.

Title: Modeling aesthetic preferences: towards taking perceptions into account in oxbow ecological restoration projects
Author: Marylise Cottet, Hervé Piégay, Anne Honegger
Abstract: To address ecosystem degradation, ecological restoration projects have proliferated since the 1990s. Characterizing and anticipating public perception are two major challenges in achieving sustainable ecosystem management that is shared by all stakeholders. This is the aim of this research, applied to a specific ecosystem: the oxbow lakes bordering the Rhône River and one of its tributaries, the Ain River in its lower valley. The aesthetic preferences of an experimental population were modeled using data collected through a photo-questionnaire survey. This model relies on a multiple regression performed on the coordinates of the factorial axes of a multiple correspondence analysis. The resulting model is stable and explains 66% of the variability in the aesthetic responses of the respondents. Six visual attributes were identified to predict aesthetic preferences for oxbow lake water bodies: 1) the dominance of green, 2) the dominance of gray or brown, 3) the presence of warm and vibrant colors, 4) the presence of aquatic vegetation with irregular shapes, 5) the presence of sediment, and 6) the turbidity of the water. Some possibilities for improving the model are discussed. A validation step carried out on a representative population sample would allow this experimental model to be used in an operational setting.

Title: Use of the outputs of the ARPEGE-Climat numerical model for the simulation of a bioclimatic index up to the end of the 21st century in the Champagne vineyard
Author: Elodie Briche, Gérard Beltrando, Claude Kergomard, Hervé Quénol
Abstract: The minimum and maximum daily temperatures from the ARPEGE-Climat numerical model, used for future climate forecasting, are compared to those at a station (Reims-Courcy) in the Champagne vineyards over a "control" period from 1950 to 2000. Future temperature simulations for three scenarios, A1B, A2, and B1, allow for the calculation of the Huglin bioclimatic index up to 2100. Temperature increases predicted by the model scenarios could lead to a change in the climate type within the vineyards, disrupting the wine industry.

Title: Between dasymetric and choropleth: a typology of space adapted to the study of the relationships between health and the environment
Author: Paul Salze, Dominique Badariotti, Arnaud Banos, Hélène Charreire, Jean-Michel Oppert, Romain Casey, Chantal Simon, Basile Chaix, Christiane Weber
Abstract: The study of the role of environmental determinants on health is a rapidly growing research area in geography and epidemiology. It involves identifying the environmental elements that enable a varied and balanced diet and regular physical activity. In this context, the opportunities available (services, green spaces, etc.) differ between rural and urban environments, making the distinction between these types of spaces essential. Given the inadequacy of traditional data sources, our work aims to develop a method for defining this fundamental spatial differentiation through the mutual enrichment of existing data. The method begins by creating a spatial typology that transcends administrative boundaries and is based on land-use criteria. Combining this typology with more conventional data results in a typology of municipalities that incorporates demographic, functional, and physical aspects. The results obtained allow for a more detailed characterization of environments, and may constitute a direct measurement of exposure or an element for adjusting models in accordance with the health/environment issue.

Title: Detection of changes in very high spatial resolution images by texture analysis: application in urban environments
Author: Antoine Lefebvre, Thomas Corpetti, Laurence Hubert Moy
Abstract: The objective of this study is to develop a method capable of identifying and characterizing changes affecting small areas using Very High Spatial Resolution (VHSR) remote sensing data acquired at different times and from different sources. To overcome these constraints, the method's originality lies in comparing the texture properties of the observed objects, thus avoiding the exclusive or primary use of spectral image information and instead focusing more on the spatial information it contains. Initially, the proposed method extracts objects through region-growth segmentation, and then the different textures within the segmented objects are compared. The approach used to characterize the textures relies on an analysis of coefficients derived from wavelet decomposition of the images. This method was applied in a peri-urban environment, specifically the Rennes metropolitan area. Peri-urban areas are highly heterogeneous and subject to abrupt and irregular changes over time and space. Changes in land cover and land use that occurred between 1978 and 2003 are detected using a pair of images: a black and white aerial photograph and a panchromatic image acquired by the Quickbird sensor. The classification rates obtained, ranging from 78% to 85%, demonstrate the importance of texture for image classification using THRS. This method thus enables the detection of changes in agricultural practices on plots under urban pressure.

Title: Evaluation of the WRF regional climate model applied to the Burgundy wine region
Author: Cyril Bonnefoy, Thierry Castel, Malika Madelin
Abstract: Current climate change is impacting crops, particularly grapevines, in terms of the earliness of phenological stages and yields. General atmospheric circulation models (GACMs) are not precise enough for impact studies on vineyards. Regional atmospheric circulation models (RACMs) are necessary to reach operational scales for this type of study. In this article, we evaluate the ability of the Weather Research and Forecasting model to reproduce climate variability in Burgundy during key periods for grapevines. The test is conducted on the year 2003, an atypical year that could become more common in the coming decades. Our aim is to use this model to regionalize the agroclimatic index of growing degree days in 2003 and thus obtain an initial simulated image of the potential viticultural climate zones in Burgundy in the years to come.

Title: Spatio-temporal organization of bushfires. A comparative approach in Burkina Faso
Author: Sébastien Caillault,  Aziz Ballouche, Daniel Delahaye
Abstract: Bushfires in sub-Saharan Africa are most often considered harmful environmental hazards. Yet, it is now established that in these tropical regions, they contribute to shaping savanna vegetation. Far from being random, these fires are even integrated into the rhythm of the social lives of the local populations. The aim of this study is therefore to highlight this "management" of fire zones by examining their spatial and temporal dynamics. Two study sites in Burkina Faso were selected for this demonstration. The results show that these phenomena are not only not sporadic and random, but that they also organize themselves in a quasi-deterministic manner. This fire dynamic is thus interpreted as a reflection of differentiated management practices between rural areas and areas dedicated to nature conservation (protected areas).

Title: A structural risk of forest fires: a methodological example of a risk geography based on the complexity of systems
Author: Adrien Mangiavillano
Abstract: The structuring of statistical data according to a power law is well known in geography, particularly in urban geography. This emergent property concerns so-called "complex" phenomena. Surprisingly, it is little explored in the geography of risk. From this perspective, we address the topic of forest fires. The proposed methodological development thus falls within a theoretical and quantitative geography of risk. After a review of the existing literature, we develop methods for measuring a power law structure of historical data. Because the phenomenon emerges, depends on, and interacts with heterogeneous, non-linear, numerous variables that are aggregated differently across different areas, one consequence is considered: the inclusion of curvature in a bi-logarithmic graph (frequencies-sizes), a curvature too long perceived as an artifact. Yet, it is invaluable for geographers whose role is to differentiate spaces as precisely as possible. By invoking a case of scale covariance (as opposed to scale invariance, which concerns a rectilinear power structure), the measured curvature provides information on the balance of positive and negative feedbacks that have interacted in a given location over a specific period. Therefore, the newly proposed parameters are considered geographical indicators that express a "structural" risk of forest fires.

Title: Modeling of noise exposure in urban environments and epidemiological studies: what are the sound sources?
Author: Sophie Pujol, Hélène Houot, Marc Berthillier, Jérôme Defrance, Joseph Lardies, Séverine Bongain, Jean-Pierre Levain, Cyril Masselot, Rémy Petit, Frédéric Mauny
Abstract: Most epidemiological research studying noise in urban environments relies on models that only incorporate noise sources related to transportation or industry. However, additional sources are likely to influence noise levels. The objective of this work is to identify, among urban environmental noise sources, those likely to improve predictive models and to estimate their respective contributions. An acoustic measurement campaign was carried out on the facades of 44 dwellings located in Besançon, France. The measured values were compared with modeled values from various noise maps into which noise sources were progressively introduced. Four additional sources were selected and implemented in the predictive model: pedestrian walkways, fountains, schoolyards, and bus stops. The temporal (day-night periods) and spatial (geographic distributions of the new sources and the dwellings equipped with noise reduction systems) contribution of each source was analyzed. Many urban noise sources combine limited acoustic power with a localized impact. Some can make a significant contribution to the accuracy of noise exposure assessments in urban environments. Considering them should improve the epidemiological approach to the relationship between noise pollution and health.

Title: Accessibility simulation in the city and educational experience: the AccesSim model
Author: Matthieu Delage, Florent Le Néchet, Thomas Louail, Hélène Mathian, Sébastien Rey Coyrehourcq
Abstract: This article presents a model for becoming familiar with the concept of accessibility in urban environments. This interactive simulation, AccesSim, was developed using the multi-agent simulation platform NetLogo. After discussing the educational and scientific value of a simulation-based approach, we present the functionality of this model, along with feedback based on participation in the Saint-Dié-des-Vosges festival (2008) and the Fête de la Science (2008).

Title: From parcel shapes to agricultural uses. Comparison of the organization of agricultural landscapes in dairy and hedgerow areas (Galicia, Lower Normandy, Southern England)
Author: Maxime Marie, Daniel Delahaye
Abstract: In the dairy and hedgerow regions of Western Europe, heavily influenced by agriculture, the spatial organization of agricultural activities appears central to the structuring of rural landscapes. Analyzing the factors that determine the location of agricultural land use is essential for understanding the logic behind landscape structuring. This contribution is based on a comparison of these location factors in five study areas situated in dairy and hedgerow regions (three in Normandy, one in Galicia, and one in southern England). The results of this research show that the organization of agricultural landscapes in these different areas is governed by the same fundamental principles and that farms consistently emerge as a key level for analyzing landscape structuring.

Title: Construction of a model for the analysis and exploration of the structural properties of a transport network
Author: Eric Mermet
Abstract: A transport network is a system that connects locations within a territory. These locations are linked by paths whose modalities vary: shortest paths, bypass paths, etc. However, in the context of network structure analysis, it is necessary to understand all possible paths and their different modalities by mapping relational indicators. The challenge of such an approach lies both in the large volume of data to be stored and analyzed, and in the identification and extraction of information. Within this framework, this article proposes a model for analyzing and exploring the structural properties of a transport network. This model is based on four key elements: a computational space containing all Origin-Destination points, a measure quantifying a property using a mathematical formula, a view allowing for variation in the level of detail through zone aggregation, and finally, a legend enabling the evaluation of results by varying the color, the number of classes, and the type of value segmentation.

Title: Relocation in urban renewal projects in Saint-Étienne: What impact on the evolution of neighborhoods and the city?
Author: Fanny Léostic
Abstract: The purpose of this article is to analyze the mobility patterns associated with demolition-reconstruction and rehabilitation projects carried out as part of urban renewal in two neighborhoods of Saint-Étienne: one in a degraded and impoverished historic center, and the other in a large social housing complex located on the outskirts of the city center. Using a statistical database of relocations, completed by social housing management organizations and the municipality, the aim is to analyze the characteristics of the relocated households and their residential trajectories related to the urban renewal projects. This leads to an examination of the potential impact of these relocations on the development of the neighborhoods concerned and on the transformation of the city as a whole.

Title: Methodological approaches to the intersection between urban growth and flood risk
Author: Janique Valy
Abstract: The Brittany region has experienced several historic floods, particularly since 1995. This succession of exceptional hydroclimatic events has prompted reflection on flood risk and the reasons for the increased vulnerability of regional urban areas. The various floods have highlighted the vulnerability of certain urban areas, challenging land-use planning strategies, especially near rapidly growing urban centers. Urban expansion, studied at the sub-municipal level, is organized from an initial state of varying vulnerability. This presentation focuses on the methodologies used to analyze urban development patterns since 1950, combined with the hydrological context. This integrated approach is developed at the scale of an urban project and examines its implementation in relation to flood risk.

Title: Preventive mapping of the risk associated with "flash floods" in northern France
Author: Johnny Douvinet, Daniel Delahaye, Patrice Langlois
Abstract: The risk associated with spring and summer flash floods is a growing concern in northern France (the Paris Basin). However, few studies have been conducted on this type of phenomenon, and hydrological analyses have primarily focused on flooding caused by overflowing rivers or rising groundwater. Within the framework of this research, we propose to provide risk managers with preventative maps of flash flood hazards at two levels of observation. An initial spatial mapping of at-risk areas at a regional scale was carried out by comparing the location of watersheds susceptible to the hazard with population centers. This exploratory approach reveals that the risk is high in certain valleys due to intense land pressure. By combining the internal structural efficiency of the watersheds, measured by the RuiCells cellular automaton, with the spatial distribution of built-up areas at fine scales, it is possible to refine the regional assessment by moving to an intra-basin scale. The maps presented for several watersheds appear to be consistent with our knowledge of the area and the statements of local experts. These mapping trials are yielding encouraging results that could, in the short term, improve the consideration of this still poorly understood and underestimated risk in these regions.

Title: Towards local energy performance indicators: territorial energy labels. A first approach based on estimating daily mobility.
Author: Jean-Philippe Antoni, Yann Fléty, Gilles Vuidel, Marie-Hélène de Sède-Marceau
Abstract: The recognition of global climate change has led to a very concrete objective: reducing greenhouse gas emissions, which is itself necessarily linked to a reduction in overall energy consumption. At the local level, this perspective translates into concrete objectives for controlling and improving energy efficiency, and can be achieved through the definition of indicators to guide decision-makers. In this context, the research presented here aims to define an energy indicator useful to urban planners: it measures the "energy performance" of the different spaces within a single urban area from the perspective of the daily mobility of its inhabitants, whose behavior is assessed using normative frameworks. We therefore propose calculating "zonal energy labels." We then put forward methodological elements for a comprehensive assessment of the impact of daily mobility on the local environment, taking into account the housing component only through the integration of household density. This method is being applied to the Greater Besançon Agglomeration Community (CAGB). In conclusion, some levers for action have been identified, but "territorial energy labels" remain a tool to be used with caution. It does, however, allow for an initial energy assessment of territories.

Title: Socio-spatial transformations of Besançon: a multi-date exploratory analysis
Author: Kawtar Najib, Anne Griffond-Boitier
Abstract: This article analyzes the socio-spatial configurations of different neighborhoods in Besançon during the intercensal period of 1990-1999. This study relies on a multi-date exploratory statistical analysis that attempts to reveal the enduring and transient structures of the urban system. To this end, data collected in the 1990 and 1999 censuses provide approximately twenty indicators characterizing the IRIS (aggregated census blocks) of Besançon. Through factor analysis, we can observe the trajectories of the IRIS between these two dates according to the selected indicators. This work highlights the socio-spatial organization of Besançon and reveals a distinction between privileged neighborhoods that have become entrenched in their comfort, more disadvantaged and isolated neighborhoods, and a central axis undergoing transformation. In general, the study of trajectories helps to show the various trends in the evolution of neighborhoods, and in particular the phenomena of gentrification, impoverishment or improvement of social mix.

Title: Modeling of spatio-temporal occurrence distributions and plant epidemiology
Author: Florencia Chimard, Jean Vaillant, Jean-Heinrich Daugrois
Abstract: Point temporal, spatial, and spatiotemporal processes have been used for several years in fields such as biology, epidemiology, seismology, and neurology to model series of event occurrences. Our study focuses on the contribution of mixture models of point processes to such modeling. It also highlights the usefulness of the Bayesian approach for assessing the variability associated with certain environmental factors. The link with stick-breaking a priori laws such as the Dirichlet process is presented. An illustration is provided with the study of the spread of sugarcane yellow leaf virus. The spatiotemporal distribution of sugarcane plants infected with SCYLV is studied in a plot, healthy at planting, located in Guadeloupe. Our main objective is to characterize and then model the dissemination of SCYLV within this plot.

Title: Animated visualizations for exploring individual mobility trajectories: guiding intuition in the analysis of complex data
Author: Laure Charleux, Sonia Chardonnel
Abstract: In a study of daily mobility based on a large-scale survey, the need for a dynamic visualization tool for individual trajectories became apparent. This article describes how we built a tool that generates SVG animations from individuals' movement chains. We then propose using this tool to guide the creation of descriptors for individual mobility trajectories and demonstrate the relevance of this approach from a geographical perspective. We conclude by discussing the exploratory work opportunities opened up by this tool, aimed at understanding the subtle characteristics of socio-territorial practices related to individual mobility.

Title: Quantifying the distance from Bussière's model: monocentrism versus "acentrism"
Author: Florent Le Néchet
Abstract: This article proposes an indicator to quantify the distance of an urban region from Bussière's monocentric model. In the case of an extreme non-monocentric configuration (a uniform population distribution, for example), the term "acentrism" is used. The proposed acentrism indicator is compared with several classic indicators of urban structure (Hoover index, Moran index, slope of the rank-size law), for both theoretical and empirical configurations—twenty-five European cities are studied. The conclusion is that a multidimensional approach to urban structure is necessary, a framework within which quantifying distance from the monocentric model can be useful.

Title: Quantifying snow depths and air temperatures at the surface of a glacier: from fieldwork to interpolation, a comparison of methods
Author: Eric Bernard, Florian Tolle, Madeleine Griselin, Dominique Laffly, Christelle Marlin
Abstract: Quantifying snow depths and surface temperatures on a glacier is most often done using data acquired at specific points, with the number of points varying depending on the program. The values obtained allow for spatial generalization of the information. This step makes it possible, on the one hand, to obtain global values that will be correlated with calculations of glacier outflows, and on the other hand, to understand the spatial variations of the phenomena studied. Within the framework of a hydroglaciology program developed in the Arctic, several spatialization methods were compared to assess their quality and reproducibility. This article reports on the comparison of six spatial discretization and interpolation methods using data from snow cores and four days of air temperature observations at the surface of Loven Glacier East.

Title: The UN, geography and the map
Author: Laurent Beauguitte
Abstract: The United Nations has existed as an object of scientific study since its creation. Yet, geographers, both Francophone and Anglophone, have not known how to study it. A historical and epistemological reflection is necessary to try to explain this geographical oversight. One hypothesis explored here concerns the difficulty of mapping the UN as an object of study.
